SALARIES OF THE FRENCH TRANSLATORS OF THE DEBATES.
speechtext:
CHAMPAGNE (Wright) moved that the fourth report of the Select Standing Committee appointed to supervise the official report of the debates of this House during the present session, be now concurred in. He said : The report speaks for itself. It recommends :
1.	That the salary, viz., $1,200, now paid to Mr. Wilfrid Larose for his services as Chief Translator of the Debates be increased to $2,000 per annum, It being understood that the said chief translator shall, as heretofore, be responsible for the management of the office and the making of the index to the French edition of the Debates.
2.	That the present salary of $1,000 paid to each member of the staff of translators of the Debates, be increased to $1,500 per annum.
3.	That the above mentioned increases date from the beginning of the present session.
As chairman of the Debates Committee, n few w'ords of explanation from myself may be required in support of the action which has been taken by the committee. These employees have been petitioning the committee for a couple of years for an increase of salary. They came before the committee last year and put their claims before us. The question was fully discussed, but it was thought advisable at that time to postpone the matter. They came before the committee again this year urging that
tiiey were entitled to an increase of salary, that the salary which was allowed them was not in proportion to the salaries given to other officers of this House, and that for all the reasons set forth in their petition, they were entitled to an increase. After having fully considered the matter, the members of the committee unanimously came to the conclusion that they were entitled to some increase. The translators asked for an increase of $1,000, which would mean a salary of $2,000 a year. The committee granted them an increase of $500, which would mean a salary of $1,500 a year; this decision was unanimously arrived at by the committee, and we now come before the House and the government asking that the necessary appropriation be made. 1 need not remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that unless exceptional reasons of a serious character can be shown to the contrary, the report of the committee ought to be adopted. I think that rule has been laid down before the House and accepted on many occasions. This committee have thought fit to recommend to the House and to the government an increase in the salary of these employees. If the government wish 1o take control of these employees, well and good, I for one as chairman of the committee would not have the slightest objection ; but so long as they remain under the control of the Debates Committee the suggestions of that committee with respect to their position ought be endorsed by the House and the government. I may perhaps be permitted to remand the House of the expression of opinion which was given on 'the subject as far back as 1884, by members of the House and members of the government, who stated at that time that these translators were deserving of more salary than they were getting. I might quote Mr. Coursol, Sir Hector Langevin and the Hon. Edward Blake, who expressed the opinion that these gentlemen were not sufficiently rewarded l or their services. Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope the government will take steps to carry the recommendation of the committee into effect. We may be told that it is rather late in the session. But I may say that in 1900 we came before the House with a report recommending that the remuneration of these translators be increased by $250 on account of the unusual length of that session. It was not then considered too late in the session to take action. The report was adopted by the House on July IT, and prorogation took place the next day. I have no doubt, that if the government desire to lie fair towards these gentlemen they wdll take the necessary means, either by inserting an item in the supplementary estimates or otherwise, to give them the increase to which we think they are entitled.

LaRIVIERE (Provencher). Mr. Speaker, this question of the indemnity

which is allowed to the translators is not a new one, because I remember very well that for the last ten or twelve years, or since I have been a member of the Debates Committee, this same question has been brought to our attention. Though the committee felt they would be justified in recommending an Increase of salary to these gentlemen at a time, I may say, when the work performed by some of them was not satisfactory, the committee did not take action on account of a certain element that then was on the Board of Translators, and on account of the dissatisfaction which they had created by the work they were performing. The whole board, I may say, has since been reorganized. We have now men who are perfectly qualified to do the work, who do the work and do it well. The fact of the matter is that for two or three years we have had a translation that is remarkably good and very acceptable to hon. members. The committee, having looked into the matter, have thought that now was the time to do justice to these gentlemen. What are they recommending 5 The committee are recommending that these gentlemen should be paid on an average the sum of $1,500. which is not beyond the maximum salary of a second class clerk. I believe that this House will be generous enough to pay these men, who are all men of high standing in literature, at least a salary equivalent to that of a second class clerk employed by the government or by this House. I believe, Sir, that though this may appear to be a pretty stiff increase, the committee has thought proper to fix at once such an indemnity to be given to these gentlemen as that they would not come back next year or the year after for a further increase. We want to settle the question for once and for all, and I think we have done so. I hope that the government and the House will approve of the work of the committee and adopt the report which is now placed before them.

maintopic: SALARIES OF THE FRENCH TRANSLATORS OF THE DEBATES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter which is more in the hands of the House than it is in the hands of the government. The House has thought proper, and with good reason, to keep in its own hands everything in connection with the reporting of the debates of the House. The reporting is not done under the supervision of the government; it is done directly under the supervision of the House through a committee which is appointed every year for that purpose. The government have no wish to offer any opposition to this recommendation, but the government will be bound to consider carefully the report of the House and give it the proper authority. I may say, personally for myself, as a member of this House, that the present committee which has undertaken for a number of years back to supervise the debates of the House, has done it in a manner that has reflected great credit upon itself. The translation of the debates some years ago was very inadequate, but the committee has adopted a new system altogether, by introducing the competitive system into the appointments. Appointments are not made now for political reasons. They are just made upon merit. Whenever a vacancy occurs applicants are called upon by the committee to pass an examination, and the most successful competitor gets the reward.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Hear, hear.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: SALARIES OF THE FRENCH TRANSLATORS OF THE DEBATES.
speechtext:
This has done a great deal to improve the translation of the debates. I remember that some years ago it was an annual complaint on the part of the French members that they could not get their reports, and that when they came they were not only late but they came in a very imperfect manner. This year I have not heard a single word of complaint and not only have I not heard any complaint, but there could not be a word of complaint, because, from my own personal knowledge of the translation, it is very well done. I do not think that it could be better done in the short space of time which the staff has to do it in. They are keeping to the point and they are now doing the work in time. They are never behind. For all these considerations, for my part, I would be very glad to favour the adoption of the report. I may say, however, that I am afraid we could not give for this session the desired increase. We are, as we hope, within a few days of prorogation, the estimates are all prepared and

in the hands of the printer to be introduced here at a very early date and it would be extremely awkward and perhaps would retard the blessed day of prorogation if we were to reopen them for this question. With this suggestion and with these observations, I have no objection that the report should be adopted.
Motion agreed to.

North-west Mounted Police, $100,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OP THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: There ought to be an explanation of this additional estimate.

Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). The appropriation last year for the North-west Mounted Police was something like $400,000 or $450,000. This is an appropriation for 500 men at $800 a year. We were not able last year to keep within the appropriation, and this was due to two causes. First, we were obliged to increase the number of stations, as we have a very much larger area than before to police. We have 86 police stations, distributed all over the territories, as compared with 83 in previous years. The largest number of stations are on the boundary between the territories and Montana and Dakota, where we have to keep a larger force on account of the increasing communications between the two sides. Then, in the Macleod district, where there are large ranches, we have a very large force, which we have not been able to decrease. There are also several Indian reserves in this district which require constant supervision. Then we had to put up a new station at the eastern boundary adjoining Manitoba, where railway construction is now going on. We have also to keep up a large number of stations north of the Saskatchewan towards the Mackenzie river. Great Slave Lake Is the station furthest north, and probably we will require a new station at the mouth of the Mackenzie. We are covering the whole of the territories, which causes larger expenditure in

travelling expenses, as we have to keep our men continually on the move. At Regina we have about 60 men, at some points ten men, at other five, and at the majority of stations one or two men. These men have to be kept moving all the time. If we could keep the men always at the same stations, the expenditure would be very much decreased, but in order to properly police the territories, and keep the force well disciplined, the men have to be constantly on the move. Another cause of increased expenditure is the changes in the force necessitated by the drafts on it to supply men for Africa. The force has proved the best nucleus for the different contingents that went to that country. The material of the force is not better than that obtained elsewhere, but the men have the advantage of expei'ience, and of being accustomed to the use of horses and being able to shift for themselves under all circumstances. For the last three years we have been depleting the force on this account and taking in raw recruits, who had to be instructed, and could not give as good service as the veterans. This has obliged ns to keep up a system of recruiting, and a system of moving the men about more than would otherwise have been necessary.

Perhaps the minister would tell us on what principle he grades the salaries. He is paying men all the way from $500 to $3,000 a year, and he ought to he able to explain how he arrives at the amount in each case.

They are supposed to be paid according to their capacity and ability to do the work. If salaries are raised it is because of satisfactory and efficient service, just as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) would raise the salary of an efficient man who was working for him.

I do not think that is a very satisfactory explanation. Mr. Devlin, for instance, is only an ordinary immigration agent in Ireland-at least, that is the statement made in this House and to tne committee ; yet he is paid $3,000 a year. Yet, Mr. Preston, who has charge of the whole business over there, is only getting the same salary. The deputy minister, who is at the head of the whole department, only gets $200 a year more than Mr. Devlin, while the superintendant of immigration gets $500 less. It does seem to me there ought to be some explanation why a man who is given a small territory should be thus singled out. I recollect very well the minister's speech when this was up before the House on a former occasion, when he spoke of Mr. Devlin's great ability. But if this officer is such an able man, surely the minister ought to give him something else to do than to fill the place of immigration agent in a small territory, from which, as I am reminded by an hon. friend near me, he secures but few immigrants anyway. The expenditure on the service _ in Ireland was about $18,000, and, according to Mr. Devlin's own report, the immigrants he and his fellow agents secured from Ireland numbered only 953. There is a question or two I wish to discuss with the minister, and they can come under this head I think. I would like to know if it is the intention of the governmjenlt to pay over certain moneys to the provincial government of Manitoba, certain accrued interests, and if it will be necessary to introduce legislation in order to do that ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, i am not in a position to say positively. I know it has been decided to pay the money over, and I think the Department of Justice is considering whether legislation is required. I can see the Minister of Justice and give an answer this afternoon.
I understand a deputation waited on the minister when he was in Winnipeg, and lie promised to pay this interest ; but I think lie also told them that legislation would be necessary.
That is quite true ; I remember saying on different occasions that legislation might be necessary, and my recollection is that the question was referred to the Department of Justice.

I think I can satisfy my hon. friend about tills. The matter is in the hands of the Department of Justice at this moment. I understand their opinion is that it is simply a matter of book-keeping ; it is not money of this country, it is money that belongs to the province of Manitoba.
I have no final report, but that is my impression now. At all events, the matter has not been forgotten, we are dealing with it.

There is another question in regard to the sale of school lands that took place some time ago in Manitoba. I would like to know if the minister could tell me how many of those sales he has cancelled ?

That is not a question which I can answer now. But there is no difficulty about ascertaining the number of sales cancelled, the names and the parcels of land referred to, and I can give the information to-moi'row.

There is a certain sale 1 wish to discuss with the minister, that is the sale of the North-west quarter of section 11, 8-14 west. Has the minister any information regarding that particular sale to show whether a man named Thornbury gets that land ?
I could not answer a question like that without looking at the records. I can tell the hon. gentleman this afternoon.

We will drop that for the present. Then there is another question regarding the interest on the sales of school lands, which interest was lowered from 6 per cent to 5 per cent. Now, as we understand it in Manitoba, and as the Premier has said, the money, or the land either for that matter, does not belong to this government, they are merely acting as trustees. Well, those lands have been sold in the past, and on the last sale that took place it was advertised that the interest should be 6 per cent. By an Act passed last session that interest was lowered to 5 per cent. The Minister of the Interior, in his speech last session, said that the interest on Dominion lands should be lowered to 5 per cent. Well, the school lands are not looked upon as Dominion lands, and when the minister made that statement in the House last session it was not understood that it was to affect the sale of school lands. The effect of that arrangement is to take $25,000 a year out of the funds of the province of Manitoba ; and the effect on the last sale has been that the men who bought those lands expecting to have to pay 6 per cent find that, by the generosity of this government, they only have to pay 5 per cent. I think that the government of Manitoba and those of the people who are not benefited feel that they are losing to that extent. If those people who bought the land were aware that this was to take effect and that they were to he affected benefically by it they certainly had information that enabled them to pay higher prices for the land than
others who were under the impression, that, according to the advertisement, the rate of interest was going to be 6 per cent.

The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has admitted that the Dominion government are only acting as trustees for the Manitoba government so far as school lands are concerned. In that case I think it would have been only proper and fair to have consulted

the provincial authorities as to the reduction in the rate of interest when they were acting" as trustees. The Dominion government have reduced the rate of interest without consulting the local authorities in Manitoba. These school lands do not belong to the Dominion government, they are simply acting as trustees and I think it would only have been proper to have consulted the local1 legislature as to the reduction in the rate of interest. From one point of view what the right hon. gentleman says may be correct. If it is the settler who derives the benefit there would not 'be very much objection, but that is a disputed point, because, at any sales of school lands, speculators have been the purchasers and they have derived the benefit. If we were assured that the settlers would derive the benefit of the reduction in the rate of interest we would not Object, but these speculators have purchased the lands and they have derived the benefit. We would not object so much to the reduction of interest in the interest of the settler, but so far as making the reduction was concerned, I think it was not fair to include sales that had already taken place because the purchasers bought under certain terms knowing that they would have to pay 6 per cent. We object to an Act of parliament being made to apply to past sales and we also say that the provincial authorities should have been consulted before any reduction in the rate of interest was made as this reduction entails a loss of $25,000 per annum to the province.

The statement was made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), and it certainly has been made in criticising this transaction in other places, that the beneficiaries of the change in the rate of interest were the speculators who purchased the land. There is absolutely no foundation for that statement. I have at this moment figures in my possession which prove that practically all the land that was affected, almost all with the most trifling exceptions, was purchased by actual settlers, men who live either on the adjoining land or in the neighborhood of such land, so that the reduction in the rate of interest has enured, practically, almost without exception, to the benefit^ of actual farmers and settlers in the neighbourhood. I need only say one word as to the question of what the Obligation of the government is. I have always taken the position that the province ought to benefit as largely as possible by this fund.
I have always taken a strong position in that respect. I very cordially favour the province deriving the largest possible benefit from the fund. In regard to the money we were discussing a moment ago, that is the interest accruing on the deferred payments, I very cordially favour that accruing to the province to the greatest possible extent. But, it must be remembered that this government have been

charged with a duty in connection with the management of this fund. The province is not responsible in any way. W e are responsible for the rate of interest charged against the people who purchase the land, and for my part, I think, in view of the general reduction in the rate of interest all over the country, a reduction from 6 to 5 per cent, it would have been quite indefensible, it would have been taking a position! quite impossible to satisfactorily explain or defend, if we had still required persons who are owing us in connection with these sales, to have paid 6 per cent. I am quite satisfied, speaking as the head of the department, that the result simply would have been that there would have been an interminable correspondence with persons who had purchased that land making claims for refunds on the ground that they had not been fairly treated, with the result that somebody ultimately would have had to have given way. I felt that the question should be considered. I think the change will prove a benefit to the provincial government in the long run. I believe the reduction will produce more money because the principal money will 'be larger by reason of increased sales and this will more than counterbalance any reduction in the rate of interest. Whether that is so or not, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) will agree with me that the action of the government in reducing the rate of interest from 6 to 5 per cent has been worth a great deal of money to the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories in view of the general effect it lias had in the reduction of interest, because, as the hon. gentleman knows, the amount payable in interest by the people of the west is a very heavy charge.

Excise, $7,000.

I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Inland Revenue to the importance of doing something with reference to the weighing of grain coming from the threshing machine. This is a matter which is of much greater importance than the department seems to think, and I just wish to refer to a case which occurred in court on account of this. This clipping is from the ' North-west Farmer.'
At Nepawa the other day, John H. Howard sued T. Poole and John Dueklow, for Lis threshing bill. Both of them set up the usual defence that the grain was not measured In accordance with the Dominion statutes, and therefore they could get from under their obligation to pay for the work. This defence of course blocked the court from dealing with the case on its (merits, and the plaintiff was nonsuited.
As I have mentioned to the House before, it is altogether impossible to deal with these threshing machines and measure the grain according to the standard prescribed by the department. You could scarcely put enough men with bushel measures around one of these threshing machines, which put out from 2,000 to 3,000 bushels in a day, to measure the grain. These machines are provided with automatic measuring appliances, and I think the government should instruct their officers to use these before the next crop is threshed, so that this injustice may be removed. It does not matter what bargain a man may make with the owner of a threshing machine, all he has to do is to fall back on the plea that the grain was not weighed according to the Dominion statutes, and refuse to pay. Here are two men who avoided payment iu this way, although they understood perfectly the system and the bargain that was made with them. It is a great injustice, and it will be a great hindrance to the country if we have to go back to the primitive style of handling grain by means of the ordinary bushel measure.

Some years ago oue of our inspectors was instructed to inspect one of these weighing machines, and it was found to be so imperfect that he would not certify to its results ; but recently I have received information that within a short time a proper scale will be perfected, for attachment to weighing machines, and will he ready for use next season. Some weeks ago a manufacturer of these weighing machines was in the department, and from the way he spoke, and from information which we have received from our own officers in Winnipeg, we are in a position to state that within a few months, or before next session opens, that difficulty will be remedied.

The last time I had a conversation with the hon. minister



lie mentioned that an officer of his in Winnipeg was coming to Ottawa with a new machine. Has he arrived yet ?

Not yet. We expect him within the next week or two. He says that the weighing machine, to the best of his belief, is perfect, and will be ready to be attached to threshing machines within a few months.

000.

speechtext:
The total estimated expense of this contingent is $80,000. We are asking for $30,000 to be expended in the current year ending 1st July next, and, in the supplementary estimates for next year, which are to be brought down in a day or two. there will be an item for $50,000. The estimate is made up in this way: A contract has been made with the Allans to convey the contingent from Quebec to Liverpool and back, at $50 each for the men and $120 each for the officers. There will be 580 men and 22 officers. The transportation across the ocean will cost, therefore, in round numbers, $30,000. Railway transportation to Quebec, the point at which the force will be mobilized, together with subsistence in transit, is expected to cost $15,000. Pay for 45 days is estimated at $17,000. As for clothing, of course the ordinary militia clothing will be used, but, in some cases we shall need to make alterations and also to issue new clothing. The cost of this is estimated at $10,000. Contingencies will take about $8,000. These items make a total of $80,000. I may say that the JubiJee

Contingent cost $30,000. It was made up of something over 200 officers and men. In this case, there will be a little over 600 , officers and men.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: How is the contingent to be composed ?

The contingent has not been made up yet, but I think I can give pretty full information on that point. In the first place, there will be 300 mounted men and 280 infantry. The mounted body will be made up of 25 men from the North-west Mounted Police, 25 from Strathcona's Horse, and the balance from the cavalry, mounted rifles and field artillery. The infantry will be made up from the different branches of infantry and the garrison artillery, the infantry being composed of guards, fusiliers, highlanders and rifles. In addition to this we shall endeavour to have every branch of the service represented. There will be a representation of the bearer companies, the field hospital corps, the engineers and the new branch of the service, the army service corps, which has recently been organized.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What proportion of these men will be drawn from each province, and how will they be taken ?

They will be taken from each unit. The average number from the infantry is exactly one and three-quarters from each regiment. This will mean, of course, that the larger regiments will send two men each and the smaller regiments one man each. The squadrons of cavalry will get, I think, four men each, because the number of mounted men is larger in proportion than the number of infantry.

The men will be selected by the district officer commanding in each district.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

Supreme Court of Canada-allowances to ad hoc judges, $800.
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. William Paterson).

speechtext:
Do I understand that this is going to be paid ? I do not see how it can -be paid unless my hon. friend goes on with the Bill which provides for the appointment of assistant judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. I -call attention to the fact that there is a pressing necessity that this Bill should be passed this session. There are several cases, I understand, on the list of the -Supreme Court in which two of the judges are not competent to sit. They are cases in which the government is interested and upon which these gentlemen passed when they were ministers of the Crown. I would quote a case which is a precedent in these matters. Sir Alexander Laco-ste, Chief Justice of the Court of Appeals for Quebec, was appointed administrator of that province at a time when the late Lieutanant-Governor, Sir Adolphe Chapleau, was absent. An Order in Council came before him upon which were based contracts between parties and the government. When these contracts were before the courts, -or some of them, -and suits were taken upon them, Chief Justice Lacoste refused to sit, simply because, when he was administrator, he had signed an Order in Council upon which the contracts were based. It seems to me this is a precedent for cases of this kind in which the administrator had nothing to do but to sign his name as a ministerial act. When questions come u-p before the Supreme Court involving the validity or invalidity of con-

tracts, or damages upon contracts, which were before the administration when certain gentlemen sat in the council who are now judges of the Supreme Court, these gentlemen should not sit, and I understand they are loath to sit, that they do not want to sit. On the other hand, these are important cases, and it will be delaying the business of the court if they cannot sat. As I said, I think it is very pressing that this .Bill should be proceeded with. I quite understand the difficulty, and probably it is not quite proper that the Governor in Council should appoint substitutes or judges ad hoc. But I suggest that that difficulty could be got over in the province of Quebec, for instance, if the judgments under review were judgments that came from the Court of King's Bench, that the Chief Justice of the Superior Court should have the appointing power. If on the other hand, it was a case that came from the Superior Court sitting an review, then the appointing power should be the Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench. I believe the Minister of Justice appreciates the difficulty, and sees that judges of the Supreme Court and who are likely to be called upon to sit ou these cases, should not sit, and that some provision should be made for their being replaced.

I quite appreciate the force of all that has been said by my learned friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain). I think it is extremely desirable that we should make provision for the difficulties that he has suggested. No doubt there may be some question arising as to whether some of the members of the Supreme Court should sit in cases before them. My hon. friend will bear in mind that this is a matter which is personal to the judges themselves ; it would be for the judge to say whether, under the circumstances, be felt that he ought not to sit in the oase. Far from having made up my mind not to press the Bill, on the contrary, the present intention is to press the Bill through during this session. In that view, of course, it is necessary to put this item in the estimates.

speechtext: It was a good year for the lawyers.
And a bad year for murderers. Increase in cost of maintenance of prisoners in the North-west Territories $2,500, and increase in witness and jury fees, $4,000.
That is a great deal more than $6,000. Will the hon. gentleman tell me how he paid this amount with that amount of money ?

I understand that. I understand that the $6,000 has been spent already.

I understand that perfectly. The hon. minister had a grant for this purpose last year and he has over spent it by $6,000.

No. I will have exceeded it at the end of the year by $6,000. Additional amount required lor witness and jury fees (Governor General's warrant, $12,000), $15,000.
In this case you have obtained money under Governor General's warrants.	.

Of the amount that is required, there will be taken $13,000 to cover the cost of the disbursements in the case of O'Brien, and there will be for law books, $1,500. Hon. gentlemen will remember having heard of this O'Brien case as one in which O'Brien was convicted of deliberately murdering three men on the trail between the frontier and Dawson city. He had built for himself a shack on the side of the road and he lay in wait for people passing up and down and in this way he succeeded in disposing of three men. The men disappeared in the month of December, 1000, and their bodies were not found until the spring of 1901. It took a very considerable time to get together the evidence necessary to bring the crime home and as a result the expenditures made by the officials were very great. For instance, there was paid in connection with the case for witness and jury fees, $13,233, stenographers fees, $284, and cost of the execution, $586. In addition to that the North-west mounted police were obliged to spend something like $22,000 on the case so that the case will cost the government something in the vicinity of $40,000. But, I think the money was well spent, because it goes to demonstrate the fact that within the limits of Canada, wherever a man may happen to be, life and property are safe and that murderers are invariably tracked and discovered.

' Hon. Mr. HAGGART. What arbitration was that ? I never heard of it.

This farmer lives in the vicinity of St. Vincent de Paul, and owing to a sewer which was constructed by us, his cattle were injured and killed and other damage done and he claimed $4,000. A petition of right was issued, but we thought the speediest way of disposing of the matter was to appoint an officer of the court, and Mr. Cameron, the Registrar of the Supreme Court, after malting inquiry, found that Mr. Lussier was entitled to $1,922, which included witness, fees, costs, damages and everything.
To pay J. E. Farewell, K.C., balance of costa as solicitor for Judge Dartnell, upon North Ontario recount, $36.91.
How did this come in ?

This is in connection with the recount that took place in North Ontario in 1896. A recount was asked for before Judge Dartnell and an injunction was applied for in the High Court asking that he should not proceed with the recount. Judge Dartnell pleaded that he was acting as an officer of the House of Commons and that he could not be restrained by an injunction, which contention was upheld by Judge Robertson. The costs amounted to $66.37, and $29.46 were taxed against Judge Dartnell's side. Judge Dartnell holds that he was not obliged to pay his lawyer, because he was brought into court as an officer of this House.
My recollection is that there was some dispute as to which judge the recount should be before.
Is it not a bad precedent to allow a judge cost for anything of this kind ? He has no right to appear by counsel.
I think it is admitted that in all proceedings of this sort an inferior judge would be- entitled to counsel. I know that is the case so far as magistrates are concerned.
This is the first time that I have ever heard of it in this House.
Let us hope it will be the last.

Judging by the history of the transaction, it would be well that it should be the last time, because this was a sort of political job throughout. The impression on the public is that it was a little smart Aleck trick for the purpose of holding a seat in this House.
Trent caral-To dredge shoals in Trent and Otonabee rivers, $3,500.
Is this dredging done by contract or by the government ?

We are doing it with our own dredge.
Contribution towards building of road between Lindsay and Fenelon Falls, $1,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On what principle are you making this contribution ?

The old road was flooded by the construction of the canal, and a new road has to be built above the water level, on the line of the old road. That is the recommendation of our engineers and the member representing that county was strongly of opinion that the work was necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On this item I drew the minister's attention to the Poon-amalee causeway in the township of Elm-si ey, which is ih a similar position. The principle under which the government makes these contributions is that if any government work causes a portion of a road to be overflowed, 'which would not be overflowed otherwise, the government makes good that portion.

We have come to an understanding with the municipalities in such cases as the hon. gentleman mentions, and in other cases in which the raising of the water of the canal has rendered some bridges too short or unfit for use, we make a compromise with the municipalities and agree to bear a part of the cost.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: A petition was presented by the municipalities in the township of Elmsley asking for assistance for the repair of a highway which was in existence before the Rideau canal was built. They ask, and I think very fairly, that the government should grant assistance for the repair of the highway to the extent of the damage done by the government. I understand that the officers of the government have inquired into the matter and I want to know what the government intend to do.
I have not the papers, but I will get t-he information later.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to complete the Trent canal so as to connect the Georgian bay with Lake Ontario ?
We have already under contract the stretch between Lake Simcoe and Balsam lake, but we have not at present concluded that we will carry the work beyond that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Can the minister say what it will cost to complete the canal through ' Tlie MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. Our engineers estimate that It

will cost about $0,500,000 to complete it from end to end. We have expended in round numbers about $3,500,000.
That gives what depth of water ?
Six feet.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it the policy of the government to complete the work through from the Georgian bay to Lake Ontario ?

We have determined to complete the canal between Lake Simcoe and Balsam lake. The rest is practically completed or under contract. When all that is completed we will have one more contract to enter into and only one, that is, the contract for the hydraulic lift which we propose to place in that section. Beyond that we have not come to any conclusion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It will cost $3,000,000 to complete that portion of the work.
About that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And the hon. gentleman is not prepared to say whether the government will go on and complete the canal ?
I would not like to say one way or the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The work, if incomplete, must be of little value. It seems to me that It is too large an undertaking on which to go on spending money blindly, without deciding whether it is intended to finish it or not.

To what extent we. will continue the work towards completion is a point not definitely passed on by the government, and it is quite impossible for me to make any precise statement on the subject. The northern division, the section from Lake Simcoe to Peterborough, will be the first to be completed. We are now working towards completion of the lock between Lake Simcoe and Lake Balsam, and I am in hopes that a moderate expenditure will give us clear navigation from Peterborough to Lake Balsam. The estimated cost of the whole section from Balsam Lake to Lake Simcoe is one million and a half dollars, and the engineer estimates that it will cost from Lake Simcoe to Georgian Bay $1,450,000 if the canal is extended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I hope there is no question about that.
I think probably there will not, but I cannot give a definite statement on my own responsibility.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: The hon. minister is asking $300,000 to be expended this year. Will he apply any of that vote, if an Order in Council is passed, to pay Corry & Laverdure the $126,000 due them.
If this amount is due them, they will be paid, but I cannot say whether it will be out of the appropriation for the current year or for 1902-3.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How much is [DOT]appropriated for this year ?
$300,000 is all the revote for the year to come.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is only $300,000 to be spent on the work the coming year ?
That is all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In other words only $300,000 is to be spent for the coming year ?
That is all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the minister please give us some explanation ?

I would be glad to furnish all possible information, but I can only state the fact that we do not expect in the coming year to spend more than $300,000. We would have made provision for large expenditure had we finished the hydraulic lift which we are going to place on that section and which is going to cost $350,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the one at Kirkfield.
Yes, that will be provided for another year.	[DOT]
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems extraordinary for the government to say they are going on with that work, a work which they themselves admit will cost a total of $6,500,000 when finished, of which only about $3,500,000 has been spent, and yet that they are not able to tell us whether they intend to finish the work or not. A work so gigantic as this, one would suppose, might be taken into consideration by the government with a view to reaching some businesslike conclusion with regard to it before coming to the House to ask for more money. If they are not going to finish it they should let us know, if they are going to finish it they should be able to speak definitely of their intentions and( of how they purpose to carry them out.

In my opinion the money spent on this work is absolutely thrown away whether the canal is finished or not.

This is a legacy from the great Conservative party, and was started by them for the purpose apparently of enabling them to control the Midland constituencies, and it has controlled them ever since. The lift locks now under construction, which will cost about one million dollars each, were begun by the late government. Contracts, X believe were let by the late government for the construction of these locks. Any person who will go up and see these locks will get the impression that they are great baronial castles that are being built up there in the wilderness. The canal appears to me absolutely useless for a route for navigation or transportation. There will be only five feet of water on the mitre sill, and the boats that will carry through there the products of the west, if they ever do. will draw five feet of water and carry 5,000 bushels of wheat. It would take forty or fifty such boats to carry one cargo of a large upper lake steamer.
Why does the hon. gentleman stop at fifty ? He might as well make himself absolutely ridiculous and say seventy.

I do not intend to make myself ridiculous, but I say it will take forty such boats to carry the cargo of one upper lake freighter. And if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) will consider the matter for a moment he will see that I am correct. An upper lake freighter carries 200,000 bushels of wheat. The canal barges which will use this canal will not carry more than 5,000 bushels.
Nonsense.

All the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has to do is to make the calculation. The locks on this Trent Valley canal system have a length of 130 feet, and a width of 33 feet, and they admit vessels with a draught of five feet. A calculation will show that the capacity of these barges will not exceed five or six thousand bushels, and the average will be five thousand. So, it will take forty such barges to carry the cargo of an upper lake freighter. If any one suggests that a canal with no greater capacity than that will be a benefit to the country, it will be hard for me to avoid doubting his sincerity. This canal should never have been begun, and I think the quicker the government stop spending money on it the better it will be for the country at large.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. German) shall promptly have his few incoherent remarks reported in the Peterborough newspapers, for, at a single blow he has knocked his friend Hon. James Stratton to pieces. Does not the hon. gentleman know that Mr. Stratton's stock in trade in Ontario politics has been nothing but this Trent navigation system, plus a campaign
fund ? The hon. gentleman is talking the ordinary Ontario politics from his point of view. He has lived for years on the Welland canal and has seen, intermittently, an ordinary sized schooner drag its weary course through the canal. We, of course, do not wish to say anything about that canal, but when tiie hon. gentleman sees a rival to the Welland canal starting up, we hear from him as we have heard. It is not necessary for me to say anything in favour of the Trent Valley canal. It is an accepted fact and it is to be completed. The Minister of Railways and Canals has been over the route and has approved of it. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) should have been more kind to his friend the Hon. James Stratton at this intense time in his history, and should not have given him this blow below the belt.
Hon. James Stratton is quite well able to take care of himself regardless of any canal question. So far as the Welland canal is concerned, we have not the slightest jealousy-
This will be a competitor, will it not ?

A competitor ? The ordinary mule is not the competitor of the race horse, and I think that furnishes about a fair comparison between this route and the Welland canal. The Welland canal admits boats carrying 70,000 or 80,000 bushels of grain, and it is rather amusing to find hon. gentlemen comparing with this the Trent Valley canal which will take vessels carrying not more than 6,000 bushels. I do not think any one need be at all alarmed at the competition of this route with the Welland canal.

If the Welland canal is such a wonderful navigation route why is the government spending half a million dollars more in trying to blast the rocks from Port Colborne harbour so that an ordinary vessel can get in there ? The House must remember that the Trent Valley system is not a series of locks like the Welland canal, but a magnificient chain of lakes and rivers where there is free navigation. But the hon. gentleman has completely upset Mr. Stratton's stock in trade, and his remarks shall be duly reported in the Peterborough newspapers.

I am surprised that the hon. member for Welland should make such an exhibition of himself. He is generally well informed on matters respecting this country, but the reference to any other navigation route than the ditch near which he lives seems to arouse his ill feeling. We do not wish to interfere with this ditch of his, we who have a magnificent chain of lakes, Lake Coucliiching, Lake Sim-coe, Balsam lake, Sturgeon lake and all the other great chain leading down to the

Bay of Quinte. The hon. gentleman Indulges In the comparison of a horse and a mule. Why, I understand that they employ boys to drag the several schooners and canoes that pass up and down through the Welland canal. Ours is not a canal, but a chain of lakes which vessels can navigate with a full head of steam. But in the ditch of which the hon. gentleman speaks, a rate of two and a half or three miles an hour is all they are allowed to go, for fear of washing in sand and filling up the ditch. The hon. gentleman speaks of the lift locks at Peterborough and Kirk field, and says that this government was only carrying out the work of the Liberal Conservative party. It is well known that this route was designed as a great military route. But, unfortunately, people in power, even representing the Conservative party, listened to the carping opposition of some of the old Liberals who have already been relegated to oblivion. But the carpings of these people have had the effect of causing some who should know better to believe that this is not a great work.
How deep is the canal ?
Deep enough to drown a man standing on the head of the little member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan).
How tall do you want the other fellow to be ?

I do not intend to discuss whether this is a proper public work or not; it seems a little too late in the day to enter on that question. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Germdn) thought to make a point against the Conservative party by finding fault with this work, although it is endorsed and approved by the government of which he is a supporter. He said that it was during the Conservative regime that this work was commenced. I desire to draw attention to the fact that the Trent navigation work was commenced as far back as the year 1837, shortly after the completion of the Welland canal, as it was first designed. I think that after we have been going on for sixty-five years it is too late in the day to charge the responsibility for that work to either one political party or the other. I presume that there is no man alive to-day who was in power at that time and personally responsible for that work. I merely mention this fact, because the hon. gentleman seemed to have no other point in his speech than to make a reflection upon the Conservative party.

As the canal system seems to be under review, I would like to inquire from the minister if it is the intention of the government to start another canal or series of canals between Lake Nippissing and the Georgian Bay ?
I have not heard anything of the kind. No action has been taken by council towards the construction of a canal in any direction whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can the minister tell us when the work on this Trent Valley canal was commenced, and when we may hope it wiLl be wound up ?
I am safe in saying it was commenced at least fifteen years ago. Construction has been continued in the way of enlargement and extension.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When is it to be finished down to Lake Ontario ?

The question of the lower end has really not yet been considered. There are strong reasons why it is desirable to finish the upper part at an early date. There is not the same urgency in regard to the lower end. There is a strong probability of a considerable trade taking place on the canal already built, which Will bring a great deal of traffic to Peterborough. I understand that there are several gentlemen who are looking forward to establishing industries at Peterborough in consequence of this canal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I presume the minister refers to the cereal works at Peterborough. I know that the promoters are very anxious that this canal should be extended, and I can assure the minister that while this canal will assist the proprietors of the cereal works, there are hundreds of other business institutions along that line the minister is not acquainted with, but who are just as anxious to have that canal opened up. We have along the route of that canal, and tributary thereto, a population much greater than that of the city of Montreal. Some hon. gentlemen make a great noise in this House over the city of Montreal, and demand a heavy expenditure of money for the development of that place. We do not object to that, we back up a judicious expenditure for Montreal, but at the same time we ask for some consideration for the route along these waters on the Trent Valley canal.

The minister said lie knew nothing in regard to the building of a canal connecting the Georgian Bay with Lake Nippissing. I presume that if such a work was contemplated it would naturally come under the Department of Railways and Canals.
I fancy so. If there is going to be a canal constructed between Lake Nippissing and the Georgian Bay, in my judgment that work would devolve upon the Minister of Railways and Canals.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to make any further survey to ascertain the practicability of ta route by way of Port Hope ? I urged that matter upon the government last session. I do not intend
to discuss it now, but I would like to know if any further report of an engineer will be obtained by the department ?

When the government decides that the time has arrived to take up the construction of that canal from Peterborough south, no doubt very extended surveys will require to be made. I do not think we are yet sufficiently supplied with data to enable us to say anything on that question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do I understand that the surveys will include a route by Port Hope ?
I should think so,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would direct the minister's attention to the extravagance of this firm of contractors on the Trent canal. I do not know the details of the matter so far as the minister is concerned, but I understand that the minister has endeavoured to keep down these extras. But I ca,n tell the minister that I have been upon that work from time to time, and I can assure him that there was no time that I did not see five times as many men loafing as I saw working. I cannot understand how men having a contract, and hoping to finish it aiid make both ends meet, could carry on the work as those contractors seem to be doing at Peterborough. I know whereof I speak. I see the minister has endeavoured to do his best ito keep these men up to the mark, and I congratulate him oil what he has done. I hope that for the future he will keep a tight hand on them and see that they do their work.
Will the minister tell us how much of this canal is navigable now ?
I cannot tell at the moment. The deputy will procure the information for the hon. gentleman.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That canal is navigable from the head of Lake Couclii-ching to Beaverton on the first section. Then it is navigable from Kirkfield west of Balsam Lake continuously down to Lake-field, with six feet of water on the sill all the way, a distance of sixty to eighty miles. Then it is navigable from Peterborough down to Feely's Falls near Campbellford. All the way from Peterborough to Lakefield is finished, and that section will be ready as soon as the lift lock is built. Then there will be complete navigation from Feely's Falls right up to Balsam Lake; and when the work of that lift lock is completed there will be a continuous navigation from within a few miles of the Georgian Bay right down to within a few miles of the Bay of QuintG, with exception of about ten miles at each end. It will be a canal able to carry three times the quantity of

grain that the Erie canal was ever capable of carrying.

I would be sorry to let some remarks go unchallenged regarding the size and capacity of this canal. Let me say to the hon. gentlemen who have not been there, that to-day there are steamboats plying during the summer months that are licensed to carry four hundred passengers. As to the statement of the hon. member from Welland (Mr. German) concerning the size of the vessels, I am prepared to say that, with that depth of water, flat bottomed ordinary barges would be capable of carrying at least 20,000 bushels of grain.
Twenty-five thousand bushels.

And if my hon. friend thinks over the matter he will agree with me in what I say. I know of boats with a length of 260 feet and a depth of 12 feet carrying 60,000 bushels, and beyond 60,000 bushels, and if you have a boat 135 feet long with a depth of 6 feet of carrying capacity, it is plain that you will have a capacity for carriage of 20,000 bushels. Then, in addition to that, I may say, referring to the cereal factory in the town of Peterborough, that they propose at the outset to consume 15,000 bushels of grain per day and the factory is being constructed .with a consuming capacity of 30,000 bushels per day, and one of the considerations that impelled the gentlemen interested in the concern to locate there, was the fact that they would have water communication from Midland and the elevators there for the purpose of bringing their grain down to Peterborough, and also of getting their grain from along the route of the canal. It means an immense advantage to the counties of York and Simcoe that during the summer months they will be enabled to have competition with the only railway that passes through that part of the country by being able to ship their grain down through these lakes and rivers to Lake Ontario. Two or three years ago an elevator of 1,250,000 bushels capacity was erected in the town of Midland by some American gentlemen who came there in preference to locating at the city of Buffalo. 1 know that one of the great objects of the owners of that concern in coming to Midland was the fact that they anticipated there would be a consummation of this project in due course ot time, and that they would be in a position to ship out their grain either by rail or water. If hon. gentlemen would some time during the coming summer go down over these lakes and rivers in that part of the country, they would come back with vastly different feelings than those which some hon. gentlemen have given expression to in this House.

In support ot what the hon. member for East Simcoe Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
(Mr. Bennett) has said, I would mention the fact that when the Canadian Pacific Railway were building their railway bridge at Sault Ste. Marie, the Peterborough Bridge Works Company tendered for the contract. They had to take into consideration the question of freight on their material from Peterborough to Sault Ste. Marie. The extra freight which they would have been charged for hauling their material to (Sault Ste. Marie, that is, the amount by which the freight from Peterborough to Sault Ste. Marie exceeded the rate from Belgium to Sault Ste. Marie, would have been an enormous profit on their contract. It would have represented all the profit they would expect to get on their work. The freight rates from Belgium to Sault Ste. Marie were so much lower than the freight rates from Peterborough to Sault Ste. Marie, that the Peterborough Company lost the contract. If this canal had been opened it would have been an easy matter to have had that work done in our own country rather than have foreigners tendering for it and driving our people out of business. I simply mention this as one instance. Besides the town of Peterborough along the line of the canal, there are Ash-burnham, Bobcaygeon, Eenelon Fulls, Lindsay, Barrie, Orillia, and the villages of Beaverton, Campbellford, Frankford, and other towns and villages along these rivers and lakes where industries ure springing up. The freight rates will be kept down by the competition between the canal and the railway companies. We know that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, having been over this route, appreciates its importance, and I am only sorry that hon. gentlemen who are not in sympathy with the carrying on of this work are not alive to their interests. They have railway passes. Why do they not take a trip over the route, so that they may see for themselves the immense advantages that would accrue to the country from the construction of this work.
I understand that there are 60 or 70 miles of this canal now navigable. What tonnage has passed through it ? Has any record been kept of the tonnage ?
This is largely upon the lake sections. There is a navigable course from the head of Pigeon Lake down to Buckhorn and Chemong lakes, a distance of 50 miles.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will turn up the statistics in the report of the department, he will find all the information that we have.
Carillon and Grenville canals-to rebuild guide pier, $23,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is that work ?
This is a revote. We have not been able to secure the construction of this pier (luring 1901-1902, and we have therefore only expended $7,000 of that vote.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the work being done by contract ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Who are the contractors ?
They are a Toronto firm. I cannot remember their names.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see several places in these estimates, and I think it is a defect in them, where an item is stated as a revote, while in other places it is not so stated, and we are left in the dark as to how much is a revote and as to how much is an original vote.
It is omitted in some cases, but where it is omitted I inform the committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILAVAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it should be stated in all cases in the estimates.

So it should. AVhere it is only partly a revote, it should be stated what portion is a revote and what portion is an original vote. I am trying to have that done.
Quebec canals-surveys for establishing boundaries, $1,001.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: AVhat does that mean ?

It has been recommended by the officers of the department and by the chief engineer that we should have a small appropriation so that where disputes occur as to boundaries between our property and adjoining property we can make a survey. When these disputes come up we have no money that we can use for the purpose of providing for surveys.
Culbute. canal-damages by flooding, $250.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is to provide for damages by flooding in the town of Bryson, caused by the construction of a dam.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That dam has been down for a number of years. How can it have been caused by the construction of a dam ?

The hon. gentleman does not mean that the dam is down ? There was an attempt made to blow it up which made some break in it, but the dam is still there. It must have been sufficient to have occasioned this flooding. We had the matter inquired into and there was an arrangement between the town of Bryson and ourselves to settle for $250.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Here is another item of the same kind. There was a vote of $265 last year and there is a vote of $250 this year. We have no information as to whether that vote of last year was spent and this is a new item or whether there was only a small portion of the vote spent last year and this is a revote of the balance.
This is entirely a new item. The account will show that we spent nearly the whole amount that was expropriated last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is this the last claim for damages ?
There are quite a few still outstanding.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you adjust them by arbitration V
We have our valuator, and he reports his recommendation and some have not yet accepted what we considered to be fair, but possibly they will do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can the minister tell us how much we have paid for damages in this matter and what claims are still outstanding ?
I will have such a statement prepared.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What final estimates have not yet been completed on the Soulanges canal.
Those of Ryan and Macdonuell ; Andrew Onderdonk and the Canadian Electric Company. The final estimates of the others have been prepared.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In connection with these railway items, I asked the minister the other day whether the building of the railway from Charlottetown to Murray Harbour had been let by public tender and contract, and the minister said it had. I see by the papers brought down in the other House that only 21 miles of this railway had been let by tender.
Eleven and one-half miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
And that the contract for the rest of the road was given to the party who obtained the contract for the 11J miles by a mere extension of their original contract. The minister led me to believe that the whole contract was let by public tender to the next lowest tenderer ;

tlie lowest tenderer not being able to carry out. the work. I protest against such a mariner of letting contracts. Where there are 40 miles of road to be built the law requires, and the Order in Council requires that all work should be let by tender.

Tenders were first asked for 11J miles which was a distinct section of the line and the least expensive and the handiest to construct. After the work was in progress, and it became necessary in the opinion of those who were most anxious to see the work carried forward-members of parliament and members of the government-that the work should be proceeded with, an offer was made to the contractor to continue the other 31J miles at the same price for that class of work. Some dispute between the engineer and the contractor arose which led to delay and although the prices were actually settled, I am not sure that the contract has been yet finally executed by the contractor. A number of tenders were received for the work when it wras first offered, and it was thoroughly advertised in all the newspapers from the 15th of November to the 23rd of December. The prices were the schedule prices, as usual under such circumstances. When we were being hurried to get the work proceeded with we proposed to the contractor who is a very respectable man, and who had secured the first contract after open competition at prices that were fair and reasonable ; we offered to him to continue the work because for the further reason we did not wish to 'have two men operating together one at one end of the line and the other at the other end, and our proposition was accepted. The work will toe continued by the same contractor who had the first pant of the road.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

No, not carried for a while yet. You have a habit of crying ' carried ' when a member is on his feet. I had cause to draw your attention to it before, but I hope I will not again. The minister states the contract was let for 111 miles, and on the pressure of members of parliament in that section of the country and others, it became a necessity to push the work forward and the 311 miles was given to the contractor at the schedule prices which he obtained by competition for the other 111 miles of the road. Was that contract offered to him with the consent of the council at the time ?
Yes.
