speechtext: Well, all I can do is to protest against it. Here is a contract for the construction of 311 miles of railroad given to a person who has not tendered for it, and without any open competition at all ; and the only excuse the minister has is that the man had constructed another section of the road, and that it was done at the urgent request of the members of parliament representing that section of the country. What is the use of having an Act of parliament which says all such works shall be let by contract'! What is the use of the Order in Council if the minister can override it 1 We cannot do anything but protest against such extraordinary conduct as that of the minister.

There is not much use of my hon. friend talking about extraordinary conduct. He does not deceive anybody, because he must recollect that it has been a very customary and usual thing. It was so under his own administration, and if he desires to be furnished with instances of it, I will supply them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would be delighted.
The hon. gentleman may assume that what he did is not a justification, and I quite admit that it is not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to see the hon. gentleman give a justification in a particular case ?

No doubt it would hot be sufficient for me to show that the same thing has frequently occurred, and properly and naturally so. We invited offers from these tenderers, and the prices at which the contracts were awarded were fair and reasonable prices, as anybody will know who has had experience in business of that kind ; and the contractor was a very responsible man who had done a large amount of work, and upon whom one could rely as able to carry on the work in accordance with the contract. When the prices were fixed by competition on a small section, wTe could not do a wiser thing than continue the contract in the hands of a safe and responsible man for any further mileage we had to construct ; and that is what we did after the matter had been considered in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We heard of so many extraordinary acts on the part of this government that one is hardly surprised at anything that occurs ; but this act overtops everything else.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. The last is always the worst.
42S5

But one shudders to think of what the next may be. What are the facts ? The minister wished to have constructed a certain line of railway in Prince Edward Island. Tenders were asked for 111 miles in the open market. No one can find fault with that. The work was proceeded with. The 114 miles were constructed, not for a lump amount, but on what is known as schedule prices, that is, so much for this part, and so much for that part. Then, the minister deliberately goes and gives the same man a contract for 314 miles of the same road, without asking for a tender or inviting any kind of public competition. I am not going to say that there was any collusion between the minister and these contractors ; but a strong inference can be drawn from this fact, that the minister knew that there was more profit to be derived from the construction of 40 miles than there was from the construction of 11 miles. The minister might have said to the contractor :	'To construct the 11 miles will
entail the removal of a considerable plant to the scene of operations, and I will tell you what I will do :	You tender a little
higher figure for Hi miles, and I will give you the contract for the 314 miles afterwards.' I do not know that that happened ; but the minister has placed himself in such a position that this state of affairs can fairly be inferred. But the minister did worse. Had he entered into this contract, and then gone to his colleagues and said :	' I have
made this contract and we have to stand by it,' it would have been a bad enough transaction on his part. But the minister is not alone to blame, because every colleague of his assented to the deal. He says he went in the open council with it, and every one of the ministers said : ' That proposition is a proper one, and we approve of it.' Contrast the position of the Minister of Railways with that of the Postmaster General. The Postmaster General on coming into office, found that his predecessor had said to the men who had contracts for carrying the mails : ' You got the contract in the open market for carrying the mail for $120 a year, you being the lowest tenderer ; and as you have invested in the equipment necessary to carry the mail, I will renew your contract at the same figure.' The Postmaster General cancelled all such contracts. That is a matter of record. He said to the contractors : ' You had a contract for three years only ; and when your contract expired, the minister who preceded me in office had no right to renew it, and for that reason I cancel it.' There was scores of such cases. But here the Minister of Railways and Canals lets a contract for 114 miles of railway, and then on his own authority, backed up afterwards by the council, gives a contract to the same man without any tender or competition for 314 miles more. There is not a tittle of evidence before this committee to show that the other
31J miles could not have been more cheaply constructed. On the schedule prices the work would cost as much proportionately for the 314 miles as the 114 miles did, while the means of access, the materials, the supplies and opportunities to engage in the work were all much more advantageous to the contractor. If there had to be blasting on the first 114 miles, 1 suppose the minister did not in his first schedule provide for allowing so much for granite, so much for limestone, and so forth. It may be that on the first 114 miles the contractor would meet with granite, whereas on the other part he would find shale or liardpan, the excavation of which would not be nearly so expensive. The Minister of Railways and Canals is certainly carrying things with a high hand. But, I do not blame him altogether for asserting himself. He has hard work to keep the job in his department. This afternoon lie was asked whether the French river navigation system was to be under his control or not, and right along side him was the Minister of Public Works, and he made the statement emphatically that if anything were done it would be done by himself. Evidently the hon. minister intends to assert himself. All I can say is that if he can get his colleagues in the council to back him up in deals of this kind, he will be asserting his position, and asserting it pretty emphatically. I am surprised that there is not an lion, member on the other side who will stand up and protest against this high-handed proceeding, but so long as the present government remain in office, I suppose the country will have to grin and bear it. I can tell the hon. minister, however, that such transactions as this will not stand the light of public discussion, and when properly ventilated, they will be visited on the heads of the present government as they ought to be.

I do not often take up the time of the House and certainly would not rise to defend anything which I knew to be wrong or a waste of public money. I happen to be in a position to know all about this road and the ground it covers, and I think I am a much better authority on the subject than the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House. The first 114 miles were let to the lowest tenderer, and the gentleman who got the contract, Mr. Kitchen, is a very efficient contractor who belongs to New Brunswick. Those 114 miles were let at the very best rate, being the lowest of six tenders and it must be evident that the contractor, who did the work, would be better equipped to continue it and complete the balance of the road than anybody else. It -is not extraordinary therefore that lie should have been given a contract for the balance without any tenders being called for. As a general rule, it is no doubt better to call for tenders, but there are exceptions, and the government has to he guided by the

428S
conditions which prevail, and certainly in this case the contractor, having taken tlm first 111 miles at a lower rate than anybody else offered to do the work for, and having done the work efficiently and being equipped on the ground with all the appliances to continue it, it seems to me that it was a wise policy to give him an extension of his contract at the same rates. For the balance of the 31 miles the conditions are about the same. If anything, I should say that they are more difficult, because the country is a wilder and a rougher one to traverse and will require more excavations than did the other portion of the line. For my part, I am thoroughly convinced that the arrangement was a very good one, and I certaiaily would not find any fault with the Minister of Railways for having acted as he diid.
Mr. SPltOULE. The defence made by the hon. gentleman for West Queen's (Mr. Farquharson) may be a very good one from his standpoint, if he knows all the conditions and surroundings. But what we object to is the adoption of an unsound principle, and one which is contrary to that adopted as one of the planks of the Reform platform. The Reform party adopted as one of its planks that no public money should toe expended on public works except after calling for tenders and giving the contract to the lowest tenderer, and the Minister of Railways has acted in open violation of that principle. Evidently a small contract was given to this contractor in order to afford some apology for extending that contract and giving him a larger one. The hon." member says that the cuttings are heavier in the second portion perhaps than in the first. Well, that is a reason why the contract could be taken at a cheaper rate. If the haulings are shorter and the cuttings heavier, the work could be done for less money, and if tenders have been called, in all probability it would have cost less. But the great thing against which we protest is that the principle set down in the Reform platform, as one of those on which hon. gentlemen opposite would act, if returned to power, has been deliberately violated.

The hon. minister's statement does not agree with the return brought down in the Senate. He says that before this party began the work, the minister obtained the consent of his colleagues to the contract. If I remember rightly in the return brought down to the Senate, the department did not know at all that there were any such contracts entered into, and that the work had been commenced and in progress a number of months before the consent of the hon. minister's colleagues was obtained. The statement of Mr. Scott in the Senate was that the work had been in progress some time before the Order in Council was obtained authorising the contract.

We have arranged that he shall do the track laying and the ballasting.
I have not seen all the answers or statements made in the other Chamber with regard to this matter, but I know whereof I speak when I say that the extension of

this contract was made by Order in Council long before a blow was struck on the additional thirty and a half miles. I defend the extension of that contract on the ground of public interest, and I invite lion, gentlemen opposite to take the very first opportunity-it may not be available at this moment, but it will come-of entering upon the most thorough investigation of the whole proceeding. What are tenders asked for ? In order that we may make sure that the country is not paying an unreasonable price for the work that is being done. And what kind of people do you wish to tender ? People who are competent to carry out the work they undertake, people who have means, people who are responsible and can stand behind the undertakings they make. We had tenders for eleven and a half miles which was all we expected to build at that time. These tenders showed us just *vhat competition would do as to the cost of the work. Our engineers were satisfied that the prices were reasonable. And hon. gentlemen opposite can look at them and see whether they are reasonable or not. We found that we had a competent and responsible contractor, and he was willing to take the work at the same prices for similar-classes of work as those covered by his tender. Therefore, in the public interest, we did what has been done in the department over and over again, we extended this contract. I do not carry the details of these matters in my mind, but I will bring a statement of some extensions that have been made from time to time by our own and other governments, for such extensions have been made by all governments under conditions which are practically the same as these. It is a very legitimate mode of doing business for the lowest tenderers are often people who are not capable of carrying out the work, and who give the department more trouble than the saving of expense is worth. They get a contract from the government and think they are going to make a great deal of money whether they have had experience or not. But it is always better, if possible, to get a safe man. If you are paying only a reasonable price for the work and have responsible men who are capable of carrying out your contract, it is far better to extend their contracts than to call in others of whose capacity you have no knowledge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the extension had been for seventy-five miles instead of thirty-one miles, would the hon. minister have given the contract ?
There was no suggestion of an extension

speechtext: I think we shall have to ask the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) to read his colleague a great moral lecture upon the duty of giving out contracts by tender only. We know how the Postmaster General has sacrificed himself in the carrying out of his principle in this respect, a principle which has been so much neglected by hon. gentlemen opposite. I expect the Postmaster General to read his colleague a severe lecture.

I do not rise to defend the Minister of Railways and Canals, but I like to see a discussion carried on with fairness. To my mind as a business man, the Minister of Railways and Canals gave his contract for the extension of the work in a businesslike way. He did exactly what the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did in the construction of their line, Tne contractors who tendered for work on that road were given contracts right along as long as their work was satisfactory. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not appear to be in harmony. One of them said that the work on this eleven and a half miles was much more difficult than the remainder, while another said that the other part was more hilly and required more excavation. The question is simply, was the second contract let for more than the work was worth ? The Minister of Railways and Canals was the judge. He knew he had got the lowest tenderer for the eleven and a half miles, and that a good contractor could not do the rest of the work for less than the price at which he gave it. So, in a businesslike way, he extended the contract for the additional mileage he required at the same schedule of prices. I do not think the country has suffered, but the opposition in this matter are trying to make a mountain out of a molehill. Before the giving of this contract labour and everything else had advanced in price, and the chances are that the minister got the best of the bargain.

The Minister of Railways and Canals is certainly to be congratulated on the fact that at least he has found one dutiful and docile supporter. The member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray) wants no more tenders asked for by the Railway Department. If the minister says it is right, the hon. member for Pontiac accepts in silent awe. This is going to be a case of hero worship with the hon. gentleman from this time out. Let any minister bring up what he chooses and the hon. member for Pontiac is ready to say that it is all right because the minister says so. But the hon. minister did not find so docile a supporter in the hon. member for West Queen's (Mr. REVISED EDITION

Farquharson). That lion, gentleman says it may have been right or it may not. I think that hon. gentleman is aggrieved- and this throws light on the story-because the contractor did not come from Prince Edward Island, but from New Brunswick.
He came from a good place.

speechtext: He certainly came from a good place to get a contract in that department. I wonder if ' my friend Pugsley ' did not intervene on this contractor's behalf? Perhaps he did. Perhaps the Prince Edward Island contractor did not secure the services of ' my friend Pugsley.' But the blissfulness of the hon. member for Pontiac is beautiful to see. If the minister gives a contract for five miles of railway, evidently he can continue it for fifty miles without further tenders, and be sure of the support of the hon. member for Pontiac. All he wishes is that the minister shall say it is right. No doubt, he will say it is right, then he is prepared to support it. Once again I have to congratulate the Minister of Railways and Canals. He has asserted his position. He came down with the Drummond County Railway deal, all signed, sealed and delivered, and threw it at his supporters and said : There it is, take it. And they did take it. He came down with the Yukon deal and threw it at his supporters without ever consulting them, although it was only a day or two before the meeting of parliament, and they said : We will take that too. Now the minister comes down with a proposition and says, I want you to understand that I am going to let railway contracts on this principle. I shall let a contract for a few miles, and if I see the prices are right, I will extend that railway indefinitely; and I shall expect you to do as you have done before, one after another, getting up like the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray) and saying amen to the proposition.

I wish to inform the hon. gentleman that I am not a slavish supporter of this or of any government. I think he is stretching his imagination when he says that I approve of everything the minister does, and am satisfied to let him go on and let contracts. I said nothing of the kind. I say that in this case I think the minister was justified. I do not approve of the principle. The hon. member, I think, has tried to misconstrue my statements.

There is only one local train per day eastward, which leaves Point L6vis at 8.15 a.m., and arrives in Campbellton at 8.45 p.m.. taking 12 hours to cover 303 miles, and going west
the train leaves Campbellton at 10.15 p.m., and reaches L6vis at 10.45 the following morning, taking over 12 hours to cover the same distance. Then there is a train going west which leaves Campbellton at 6 o'clock in the morning, and arrives at St. Flavie at 4 p.m. in the afternoon, taking 10 hours to cover 105 miles. The local service from Metapedia to LGvis westward is altogether at night. The train leaves Campbellton at 10.45 p.m., and goes over a large area at night, arriving at the different stations at 11 p.m., 12 a.m., 3 a.m., and 4 a.m., thus compelling the people to wait until very late at night or get up at early hours in the morning in order to catch the local train. What they want is that out-train should leave Point L6vis at 7 a.m. for Campbellton and that the train which leaves Campbellton at 10.45 a.m. should leave at 7 a.m., and reach Point Levis in the evening. I have presented a number of petitions asking for this change iu the service and my colleague from Rimouski has also presented a number of petitions to the same effect, and I am sure that the liou. minister will meet the wishes of the people in that locality.

speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of the hon. minister to his surveys on the Georgian canal and to .show him how entirely useless they are. The hon. gentleman must remember that in the debate in the House it was contemplated that this would be an extension of the same system of waterways which are at present in force from Lake Superior down, which is a 20-foot navigation. But the surveys are all got out and the quantities and estimates and everything else on the basis of a 14-foot navigation. We have got that in the Welland canal, and there is no use of building a new canal with a 14-foot depth of navigation. The surveys, estimates and plans ought to have been taken out on the basis of a 20-foot navigation. If the minister

has the information in his department, perhaps the engineers, on the surveys they have made, will be able to make an estimate of the cost of the 20-foot navigation, and he ought to be ready next session to supplement his report, which is entirely useless, by giving this information.

Is the hon. gentleman under the impression that we are making a survey of the Georgian Bay route for canal purposes ? We are not doing that. I quite agree that the project ought to be on a 20-foot basis, and we' are not making any survey at all. We did one year ask parliament to give us a small grant, not exceeding $10,000, to enable us to survey a portion of the canal, but we did not take the thing up as a project at all, and have not had any extensive surveys made. I am given to understand that the company have prepared plans and estimates on the basis of a 20-foot navigation to show what the whole enterprise would cost, but that information has not been furnished the, government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the hon. minister will look at his own report, he will see that Mr. H. F. McLeod, civil engineer, and Mr. Kerr made a survey in 1900, of all the locks required on the whole length of the canal from the Georgian bay down, and gave the estimated cost, based on a depth of a 14-foot navigation.

I think that that has been abandoned for some time. We came to the conclusion that it would be idle for the company to undertake the construction of a canal with a 14-foot navigation. It must be a 20-foot or not at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Galops Rapids-Deepening and widening, $50,-CCO.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I propose to make a reduction in this item. When we were discussing this matter the other day, I said we were not asking any sum for continuing the work, but

that there was $25,000, or very close to it, which we owed on account of work done before the 1st of July of the current year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Not the current year, but the year before.
Before the 1st of July, the fiscal year in which we are now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.

Yes, the current fiscal year commences on the 1st of July. ask for one-half of this present vote, and leave the appropriation standing at $25,000. The drawback previous to the 1st of July, in the current year-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, there was no vote for the Galops Rapids last year at all. Then this work must have been done before last year; and the amount is for work, you say, dome during the current year.

I beg the hou. gentleman's pardon, I stated the very reverse. I am saying that all I am asking for is a vote which will enable me to pay what was retained by drawback for work prior to the 1st of July, in the current year, or to be more explicit, the first day of July, 1901. Not one farthing am I asking for to be paid in respect of anv work subsequent to the 1st of July, 1901.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why have an expenditure without an appropriation ? Because it must be clear that yon went on and continued the work for which you had no appropriation, about a year ago.
I did not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Somebody must have done it. Surely it was done under the instructions of the engineer.

No, I want to be understood explicitly by the committee. I stated at the last meeting of the committee when this item was referred to, that the contractor
wtas notified that we were not going to continue the work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: About what date ?
He was notified before the 1st of July, 1901; and he had no authority whatever, expressed or implied, for continuing the work after that date.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why should the hon. gentleman now ask for a sum to pay him if he had no authority ?

I -must he lacking in the faculty of explaining myself if the hon. gentleman has not understood me. I say that I am not asking for anything .more than sufficient to pay the drawback that was due and retained in the department, as is usual in all contracts, for work prior to the 1st of July, 1901.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand what the hon. minister says perfectly well. Does he mean to say that the work did in 1901 amounted to $300,000 V It was a daily contract, so much per day, and there could be no drawback in paying for anything before 1901, and there was a drawback for work done to the extent of $500,000 in 1902.
No, the hon. gentleman knows that drawbacks are always deducted in forming estimates, and it is only when special application is made that any portion of the drawback is released.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then the minister will please tell us what is the amount of the contract, what is the amount of the drawback that is due on the contract, and how far does it extend back ?

The drawback is 10 per cent on over $200,000, on all the work that was done front 1897 to 1901. Ten per cent on that has been retained and is in our bauds. I do not think I can make it clearer than that. I state distinctly to the committee that I have no intention of paying one dollar for work done after the 1st of July.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then the minister must see that he is exceeding his vote of 1901 by the extent of the drawback. He expended on the Galops Rapids a certain amount of money, which is exceeded by the drawback to the extent, as he says, of $25,000. What does he want the other $25,000 for ?
The hon. gentleman cannot properly draw an inference of that kind. I ask the hon. gentleman why he says that the appropriation was exceeded, otherwise there would be no drawback retained.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think it is perfectly clear, and the minister ought to see it at a glance. There was an amount

voted for the Galops canal in 1900, in the year previous, and in the year previous to that. Then the amount he says has been expended on the 1st of July, 1901.
What amount ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The $10,000 you paid him, plus the drawback for which you are asking an amount now. Was not the total amount voted paid to the Gilbert Company ?

No. Of the $100,000 appropriation for 1901, the amount expended was about $90,000. Now, we would have been able, if the application had been made to us before that appropriation lapsed, to pay $10,000 out otf that appropriation on account of the drawback. But it was not asked for and was not paid; and the appropriation therefore for the difference between what was paid and the amount of the drawback, has lapsed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then the total amount that.has lapsed is $10,000 ?
Yes, on that year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Don't you pay the drawback for the year previous, when he is hired by the day ?

We do sometimes. Sometimes the contractor comes in and makes an application, and we go to council and get authority to pay the drawback to the cointractor. If he does not ask for it, he does not get it. In this case he has not asked for it, and therefore he did not get it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is the amount of the drawback that is due them for the three years ?
Between $24,000 and $25,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What are you asking the other $25,000 for ?
I say I am not. I am striking $25,000 out of the vote.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You are striking out $25,000 and only going to apply the drawback which is due the contractor to the first of July, 1901?
I can assure my hon. friend that I have repeated that fifteen or twenty times.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not hear what the hon. gentleman said when he was striking out the $25,000.
That was the first thing I mentioned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Resolved that a sum not exceeding $25,000 be granted to . His Majesty for deepening and widening the Galops Rapids.

I do not recall individual instances, but I know where there have been large accumulations of drawbacks and we have very often to get the necessary authority to pay them. At certain times a contractor will allow his drawback to remain a good deal longer than he will at other times. There is no rule about it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Only in part.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

This is to cover what we have paid for gathering information in respect to a railway commission.

speechtext: Was the gentleman appointed on this railway commission a railway expert, or what qualifications had he for doing that work ?

He had very superior qualifications, as far as I could judge. I inquired to ascertain where I could get a man who had been a student of economic questions, who had studied railway questions and inter-state laws regulating railways, and I found such a man in the person of Prof. McLean.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What experience had he in connection with railways ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:

an intimate knowledge of railway traffic and traffic arrangements between railway companies as would make him an expert in that line. To rebuild waste weir, $6,000.
I suppose this is about ten times the amount you ever collected in rent from the parties you supply the water to.

What policy has the government adopted in reference to this. Why should the public be called upon to contribute to building weirs for gentlemen who have manufacturing establishments on the canal. I should think that if we furnish them with water they should build their own weirs. I am not disposed to grumble about doing anything for the benefit of the public as a whole, but as the representative of a rural constituency I do not feel called upon to vote public money to accommodate gentlemen in Montreal or anywhere else. You not only keep up the weirs but you Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
build bridges across the weirs for them. Why should we do this work for private individuals ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not accfept that as an explanation at all. I do not think it is a common' sense explanation that because a grievance has existed for years past even under the administration I supported, it should be continued. If we find that this is not a paying investment we should stop it. If it is a losing game for us let those who get the benefit of the weirs keep them up. I cannot say from memory nor can the chief engineer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister, in order to protect the canal and keep it from breaking away, should see that the weirs are properly built and put in proper order; and after that any repairs upon them should be charged to the individual who is using the water.

I cannot tell how much revenue we get from them. These water powers are subject to rental-not as much, I am sorry to say, as they ought to be, or as much as we are getting under the new leases; but they are all subject to rental.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me that if these weirs are maintained by the government for the benefit of the mills, the government ought to derive at least enough revenue from the mills to keep them in repair. These mill-owners are given an advantage over their competitors if they have these weirs maintained for them at the public expense. It is no argument to say that the same thing has been done by previous governments.

I am not bringing that forward as an argument at all, although I can say with absolute truthfulness that we are repairing the weirs just as they have always been repaired, and I think it would be rather hard on the lessees of these water privileges, after the lapse of all these years during which they have used them on the same conditions, never having been asked to contribute a farthing towards their repair, if we should now ask them to repair them. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is no clause which compels you to keep them up.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister says that hitherto there has been no contribution by the parties who own the water powers towards the maintenance of these weirs-that they have always been maintained by the government.
So I am told by the chief engineer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like the minister, before the next supplementary estimates are brought, to inquire and ascertain whether that is strictly correct or not, because, if my memory serves me rightly, I obliged some of them, when the weirs got out or order, to pay, at any rate, half the cost of putting them in order.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: While dealing with this matter, I would like to refer to a subject which pertains to it, and that is the superannuation of a man named Shield^. I desire to express my appreciation of the efforts of the Minister of Railways and Canals to see that justice was done Mr. Shields. I received a communication a short time ago to the effect that the treasury board had granted him his superannuation from the date of that letter, but I would like to call the hon. gentleman's attention to this fact, that on the 12th April, 1897, Mr. Shields was notified that his services would no longer be required. A period of five years has elapsed since then, but he is entitled to the superannuation from the 12th April, 1897, and is therefore entitled to the arrears from that date to the present. I do not think that the government are treating Mr. Shields at all fairly in simply allowing his superannuation from the present day. He . should have the arrears for that period of five years, and I would ask the hon. minister to take that matter into his consideration. I have received a letter from Mr. Shields- who unfortunately is very ill, and I do not know when he may_get better-complaining about these arrears and asking that this should be made right. Now that the government have looked into the matter and found that there was unquestionably a mistake in depriving him of his superannuation allowance, I think that they ought to grant him his superannuation from the date his services were dispensed with.

The question of arrears did not present itself to my mind, and I have not passed upon it. I was under the impression that it would be satisfactory to Mr. Shields and his friends if the superannuation were allowed. The treasury board have not the power to make any allowance in respect of arrears. If, on consideration, it seems proper, in view of the representations made to us, to allow the arrears, we will have to ask parliament for an appropriation for that purpose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is one of the reasons I have brought the matter up-that it may require a vote of the House in order to give the arrears. I have a letter from Mr. Shields which I shall be glad to show the minister. While Mr. Shields appreciates the course taken by the government in granting his superannuation, he is very soli-cdtious about the arrears. I can say that the man requires them, for he has quite a family and is in ill health. He has been unable to do any work since his dismissal owing to an unfortunate accident which

occurred while in the discharge of his duties.
Railways and Canals-Collection of revenue-general-Additional amount to persons employed in the public service and remuneration to any other persons for services rendered for and in connection with passing vessels through the canals of the government of Canada from midnight on Saturdays to midnight on Sundays, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act to the contrary, $4,000.
This is made necessary by new work and increases on all canals. The amount will be required before the close of the fiscal year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

It is for all the canals.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But the hon. minister has increased the vote in the main estimates from $15,000 to $19,000 for the canals generally, and this amount could not be needed for the Soulangas canal alone.
It is not confined to that.

No, there is naturally an increase on all the canals, the Galops, Farran's Point and all.
Mr.	TAYLOR.	Why should there be
additional work to what there was before V
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I do not just recall what increases took place. But my hou. friend knows that on account of the increased wages and one thing or other, the expense of labour on our canals is growing.

The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND

The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND 'CANALS. I do not recall upon what particular	canals they	are.

The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND

m Mr. TAYLOR. But men do not have to 'pass an examination to work on the canals.

Some of them have to, I believe.
Post Office Department-To promote Henry Knauf to a second-class Clerkship, July, 1901, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $100.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is the explanation of this ?

Henry Knauf is a German. He was appointed to the service in 1877. His present salary is $1,000 a year. He is at the maximum of his class having been there from the 1st of July, 188S. He is a third-class clerk, and has not passed the qualifying civil service examination. He is an expert in the Scandinavian languages, German and Italian, and is used in the translation of dead letters.
Post Office Department-Salaries-to pay E. J. Cummings, a junior second-class clerk, in the Branch Dead Letter Office at Vancouver, provisional allowance from March 1 to June "0, 1902, at $180 per annum, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $60.

This is a proportion of a provisional allowance, the officer being transferred to Victoria.
Post Office Department-Salaries contingencies -To pay E. L. Foley, a temporary writer of the Branch Dead Letter Office at Winnipeg, provisional allowance from' January 1 to Juno SO, 1902, at $120 per annum1, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $60.

This is the same kind of case as the other. The officer is in Winnipeg.
To increase the salary of D. Sagala, a temporary packer from $420 to $600, from July 1, 1901, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, S1S0.

This is the case of a man who has been in the service since 3890. and who, for six or seven years got no increase. He brought his case to my attention the other day, and I have given him an increase of $30 a year for the six years when he was without any increase.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I am, glad the hon. gentleman (Mr. Muloek) is repenting of his sins.
Post Office-To increase the salary of Mr. W. W. McLeod, post office inspector at Winnipeg, from $2,400 to $2,600, from March 1, 1902, $66.67.

This officer became intitled to has increase after ten years' service on the 1st March of this year, and this gives him an increase at the rate of $200 from the 1st March, to the 1st July.
To reinstate Mr. Joseph N. A. Gingras, formerly a 2nd class railway mail clerk in the Quebec district, at his former salary of $720,
from July 1, 1901, and to restore him to his former status under the Superannuation Act of 1870 and its amendments, on payment of the deductions from salary prescribed thereby, his service to be considered as continuous, and to pay him a mileage allowance of $250.72 for the year ended June 20. 1902, making a total of $97.0.72, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service or Superannuation Acts to the contrary, $970.72.

Mr. Gingras was a railway mail clerk, and was accused of having purposely delayed the transmission of newspapers and having prevented them from reaching their destina- . tion. The case seemed to he made out and he was dismissed. But, after an appeal and a re-inquiry, the conclusion we reached was that the treatment he had received was rather harsh. He explained the charge away, and I have had him reinstated. This is to make up his back pay while he was in a state of suspension or dismissal.
To complete payments for post office service to June 30, 1902, $183,000.
Last year I was away, and the officers of the department did not take a supplementary estimate for enough to carry us through.
What will be the total deficit for this year ?
Something under $200,000.

Before we leave the post office estimates I would like to call to the attention of the Postmaster General a defect in the mail service between Dawson and Victoria, B.C. I have just received today from the Wholesale Grocers' Exchange, Victoria, a letter which reads as follows :-

That is all over now, it is all arranged. It arose on account of our not being able to make an agreement with the White Pass Railway. That railway underwent a change, and we have a contract signed within the last week by them and instructions have gone forward.

If the mails are made up for Vancouver as formerly some delay will occur. What the people there suggest is that the mail from Skagway and Dawson for Victoria be made up at Dawson for Victoria, so that a steamer when calling at Vancouver may bring the mails with her.

I will endeavour to do that and to see that every steamer passing between Canada and the Yukon shall take the mails, whether the steamer be American or Canadian. I have not succeeded wholly with the Americans, but I have made an arrangement that we shall have at least one service a week both ways by one of the American ships that take their own mails.

I do not think the Postmaster General quite catches the point. The difficulty seems to be that the mails from the Yukon are made up for Vancouver, all the mails are distributed there, so that a steamer coming from Skagway for Victoria calls at Vancouver and delivers the mail there, remains half an hour or so and comes on to Victoria. Then the regular steamer, if she has left previous to that time, does not get to Victoria with the mail until the following night. So it puts us twenty-four hours behind Vancouver in receiving our mail.

We are now ready to go on with the items of the Minister of Agriculture ; but as he is not present and may come in later, in the meantime, it might meet the convenience of the House to discuss the Bill respecting labour troubles. The premier promised that if possible he would allow an opportunity to discuss it on the second reading. I do not know whether any hon. gentleman desires to diis'cuss it at this late hour; but if any one desires to do so, I will move that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why take up the time when it is not the intention of the government to press the labour Bill?
There are very few representatives' of labour in the House to-night, I mean of the prominent representatives.
I think a great deal of good will come from a discussion. We do not wish to pass it through until it is fully discussed.
I thought it was already sufficiently discussed, because the government have relegated it to the next session.
I do not think many members have had sufficient time to study it
When was the announcement made that an opportunity would be given for further discussion?
On the first reading. The government was asked if an opportunity would be given for a second reading, and the premier said if possible.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would suggest to the Postmaster General, who is leading the House now, that if no other business is ready, we should take up the Bill of the hon. member for Montreal (Mr. Roddick), who is very anxious to have it passed.

It would not be advisable to take it up without notice.
Board of Civil Service Examiners, $200.
I thought it was' announced that that item would be dropped.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why hold civil service ex, animations now when thousands of people have passed and there are no places for them ?
It was ever so.

Civil service examinations have been advertised in the papers for May and November. There are a large number of young men in the country who desire to pass the civil service examination -promotion examinations', it is true, but even civil service examinations without promotion. I think it is wisdom on the part of this government and on the part of every government to adopt the principle that no person should be placed in the civil service without having passed an examination. I am free to admit that on the recommendation of party friends gentlemen are placed in positions in the civil service who have not passed an examination; but I think the government would do well to adopt the principle that no person could be appointed to the s'ervice who had not pasesd the examination. That would be an encouragement to young men to educate themselves for positions in the service, irrespective [DOT] of their party leanings. We have plenty of young men who would be glad to take positions in the service and who would qualify themselves therefor and make suitable employees, irrespective of their politics ; but the trouble is that they are set aside by party interest. I think that is wrong. I am free to say that if there were two gentlemen equally competent, one being a Liberal and the other a Conservative, so far as I am concerned, I would probably be inclined to recommend the Liberal. I suppose that is natural. But 1 would like to impress on the government the idea that it would be wise to make it a necessary qualification for all employees that they should have passed the civil service examination.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman ought to have taken the government to task a night or two ago when they passed an item here practically doing away with the Civil Service Act altogether.

I think the history of the last two years ought to be enough to disabuse the hon. gentleman of the impression that young men get into the service by reason of having passed the civil service examinations. Under the Conservative government no person could get into the service unless he had passed the civil service examination. But since this government has come into power that rule is more honoured in the breach than in the observance. The fact is, that there is scarcely an item in the estimates nowadays which does not contain the proviso ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act to the con-

trary,' showing that the appointment was made in open violation of that Act.
Charges of management-additional amount required for printing and engraving Dominion notes, $25,000.
Was there a new contract entered into with this firm for the printing and engraving of Dominion notes ?
Yes.
Is it a private contract, or was it by tender, or how was it let ?

It was a renewal of the old contract made with the American Bank Note Company. There is only one other company that could tender; that is the Burland Company, and for reasons which I am sure will be satisfactory it was not deemed advisable to invite that -firm to tender.
Why ?
T suppose the hon. gentleman is aware of the litigation pending between the government and the old contractors.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is the government's fault.

It is the fault of the old government, my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) means. If he is at all familiar with the case I am sure he will not press the question, but if he desires to press for the information I will give it to him.
This is an expenditure involving $25,000.
It is a great deal more than that.

I mean this estimate under consideration. That is a very respectable sum. It would be natural that we would anticipate when the government were expending that large amount of money that they would endeavour to expend it in an economical way, and to do that it would be fair to let the contract after open competition.

I agree with my hon. friend, but there are only two companies on this continent-I speak subject to correction, as I am not aware of more than two companies-that do this business. There is the American Bank Note Company, that recently established here, and there is the British American Bank Note Company, which for many years had the contract. In 1897 the contract was removed from the old company and transferred to the present contractors. It was then discovered that the old company had been guilty of a breach of contract. There Is no question about that. The contract required them to supply a steel engraved stamp to the Inland Revenue Department,
but instead of doing so they mixed up lithographed stamps to a very large amount, and this deception was practised without the knowledge of the Department of Inland Revenue. Neither the minister nor any of his officials was aware that the stamps delivered were mere lithographs instead of being steel engraved, and for many years they continued to pay for these stamps as if they were according to contract. After the discovery was made the matter was brought into court, and the Exchequer Court has given judgment against the contractors for $100,000. The matter is now in the Supreme Court, and in view of that kind of treatment received by the Dominion of Canada the present government are not prepared to invite these former contractors to tender for the performance of such work.
What is the total amount involved in the contract every year ? What is the amount paid the American Bank Note Company for work done under their contract ?
It is a varying sum. It is so much an item, so much for printing postage stamps, so much for printing postal notes, Inland Revenue stamps, bank bills, &e. It is a schedule contract.
It amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars annually though ?
I do not think so much as that.
How much ?
I cannot give my hon. friend the figures.
The contract is for five years and has been renewed ?
Yes.

There are many establishments in Canada which, if an opportunity had been given to put in tenders for this work, would have done so. It seems to me to be a departure from the professions which the hon. gentleman made and which his party made many years ago that great amounts of public work should be given out without public competition. It is not at all creditable to the Dominion of Canada that work of such a nature should be done by a .firm which is practically a foreign firm and that a very large portion of this work-the finer portions of the work-should be done in the United States.
That is not correct.
It was correct when the contract was first made and we have no evidence that it is not correct now.
No.

If the hon. gentleman states on his own knowledge that it is not

correct, of course, I will have to withdraw that statement. Does he state that none of the work of this contract in engraving is done in the United States ?

X do not see the work done, but I believe that none is performed except in Ottawa. When the contract was taken in the first instance, until the company got into working order, a very limited portion of the work was allowed to be done in the United States, the engraving of the die and the steel rolls, but I have seen in regard to work for my department part of that work done, and I see no reason wrhy the same should not be done in the case of bank notes. My hon. friend talks of this company engraving bank notes as if it were simply a matter of printing posters for ordinary purposes. It is a very responsible position, and many of the banks of Canada at all events show their appreciation of the standing of this company by employing them to do their work. My hon. friend talks about the company as if they were here to-day and away to-morrow. They have invested large sums of money in permanent plant in the city of Ottawa, they have erected a handsome building and they own this property in freehold. At one time this company did a great deal of engraving in New York for the Canadian banks, which work has now been transferred to Canada, and this company here is doing a great deal of bank note engraving for the banks of Canada which was formerly done in the city of New York.
It is an unjustifiable thing to renew a contract of this kind without ascertaining whether or not there are other firms doing similar work in Canada.
The hon. gentleman's predecessors for a generation renewed the contract with the British American Bank Note Company without a tender.
And the only apology that the hon. gentleman has to make is that for twenty years his predecessors in office did what he is doing now.
No, we have a very much better contract.
What was the difference?
Then this contract made with the new company meant a great deal where there was a difference between the two companies of $165,000.
For five years.

If the hon. gentleman was expending $165,000 of his own money I think he would not renew a contract without endeavouring to ascertain whether the Mr. CLARKE.
work could be done by other firms for a less amount. When the contract was offered to the American Bank Note Company, I know a firm in Toronto which sent its representative down here to make inquiries in respect to the work, a firm that was doing the highest class of engraving that can possibly be done, and a Canadian firm, and I think before the contract for this work which will involve $1,000,000 of an expenditure was renewed, an opportunity should have been given to Canadian firms to undertake the work and do it in this country. If the government had then found that the work could not be done as well as it is being done now, or that It could not have been done for less money than is being paid now, the government might have been justified in renewing the contract, but in the absence of that the government cannot justify its action in renewing for five years without tender a contract made five years ago involving such a vast expenditure of public money. On no business principle can the government justify its action in renewing for five years without tender, a contract which involves such a vast expenditure of public money. When the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) was in opposition he did not hesitate to condemn loudly, and properly in my judgment, anything of that kind if it was perpetrated by his political opponents.
I am glad to learn of a change of heart in the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke). We have got a most profitable contract-
For the firm.

We have a most profitable contract for the_ Dominion of Canada, a contract which saves thousands of dollars a year as compared with the contract price paid by the late government. When the present government made this contract by which we got cheaper and better work none were louder in denouncing us because we did not continue with the old contractor without renewal than this hou. gentleman and his colleagues.
No.

Yes. 1 sat in this House and heard it. The hon. George E. Foster denounced us because we had passed over the British American Bank Note Company which had forfeited any claim to the consideration of the government, and my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has the coolness to stand up here and to tell us to go back to the old system of for twenty years renewing a contract at improvident prices. If the hon. Minister of Finance were present he would be able to give evidence to show that the terms of this renewal are fair and reasonable. The company about which my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) speaks so flippantly is a very solvent

company, highly respectaole company, and it is doing the most confidential work in Canada for those who desire it. The banks in Canada know their own business, and if they think this company is sufficiently responsible, sufficiently reliable, and sufficiently trustworthy to be given this very delicate work of engraving bank notes, we think so to. There might be other companies that would in time grow up to the situation, but it is not every even well equipped engraving house to-day that could commence manufacturing bank bills and stamps at once. In the old country the government continues for years and years with the same contractor because of the confidential relations which exist between the two.

I had the opportunity-as my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) might have had the opportunity if he wished to avail himself of it-of visiting the bank note establishment the other day. If the hon. gentleman would visit that office he would find that all the work is done in Canada,, the steel engraving and the printing of the bank notes, by Canadians, with the exception of possibly the manager, the assistant manager, and two of the employees, who are Americans. Otherwise all the work is done by Canadian labour. In addition to doing the work for the Dominion government and apparently doing it satisfactorily, this concern is doing work for nearly all the banks in the Dominion at the present time. I am surprised at the statement made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) in view of the fact that he is a practical printer and knows as well as any man in the House that there are only two establishments in Canada that do work of that kind. You might ask for tenders all you like, but you would only receive tenders from the two establishments that are in Ottawa. I believe that the government has given a good reason why it was not advisable for them to ask for tenders from the old firm.

I am much obliged to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) for telling me how I should act and where I should go to obtain information. But, in talking the way he does he is simply beating the air.
I say that in a matter involving this very large expenditure extending over a period of five years, the government should have called for tenders as the hon. gentleman would do himself if lie were contracting to have such work done for him. How does he, or how does the minister know that Canadian firms would not put themselves in a position to do this work just as satisfactorily as the American firm if the Canadian firms were given the opportunity? How does he know that if tenders had been asked for Canadian firms would not have put themselves in a position to provide plant to do this work ? Is it a business proposition that in a contract involving nearly a $1,000,000 the government should renew ^ 130
the contract to the same firm without ascertaining whether any responsible and reliable Canadian firms could do the work ? Common business principles would lia-qe dictated the ordinary method of calling for tenders in such a case. I am surprised that a man like the hon. member (Mr. Holmes) should justify such action on the part of the government. I am prepared to say that if reasonable notice had been given and tenders asked for, more than two Canadian firms would have put in tenders for this contract.

I am not surprised to hear that the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) knows it all. No doubt, the valuable information that he has given to the House at different times has convinced the people of the country that he knows it all. However, there are certain things which even gentlemen in the city of Toronto can learn, but they require humility in order to learn it, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) who assumes a very patriotic air now is not consistent in the theory he is putting forth. I did not intend to give him information, I simply wanted to convey the idea that the information is available to any member of the House who wants to learn. Of course there are some people who are too big to seek information, and who simply make recriminations in this House for political effect, and for what they can gain by appealing to public sentiment and to things of that kind. Some of us may be sincere in the advocacy of certain principles, and some of us may be talking to the gallery as certain people from Toronto do occasionally. So far as this not being a business proposition is concerned, I assert that the government did what was perfectly right and that the people of Canada will endorse their action in renewing the contract to that firm. When the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) talks about beating the air, I can tell him that no body beats the air more than he does when he speaks of calling for tenders, because he knows perfectly well that there are only two firms in all Canada who would entertain a proposition involving this very large expenditure. But the trouble with our friends on the other side of the- House is, that this business government was able to make a contract in this manner which saved the country $150,000 in five years, and were able to renew it on equally good terms.
Why should not this government give a Canadian company employing Canadians an opportunity to tender for this work.

This company employs
Canadians.

Why should not the contract be given to a company having its interests in Canada, in preference to an American firm ?	The hon. gentleman,



speaking from a patriotic standpoint, says that we saved $150,000 in five years on this contract. But how inconsistent are hon. gentlemen opposite. The Minister of Railways said the other day that he had given a contract to a Canadian company to provide steel rails at $8 a ton more than they could be purchased for outside, in order to encourage Canadian industry. What did that cost the people of this country ? $175,000 a year. And yet these hon. gentlemen say that we are not patriotic, because we would not save $30,000 a year on this bank note business, toy giving the contract to an American company. If these hon. gentlemen are going to toe patriotic in one way, let them be patriotic in another. If they are going to spend $175,000 a year for the purpose of producing steel rails in Canada, why! not spend $30,000 a year for the purpose of producing these Dominion notes in Canada ? If the minister or his followers cannot produce any better argument than that, they are out of the race.
Will the hon. gentleman answer me a question ? Who is manufacturing steel rails in Canada ?
Clergue.

Well, Clergue is an American citizen who has come into Canada and is developing the industries of Canada. The American Bank Note Company have also come into Canada and are developing our industries in the same way.
The argument of the hon. gentleman is that Canadians are no good, and we have to depend on Americans to come in and develop our resources.
The argument is as good in one case as in the other.

The hon. gentleman does not seem to realize yet the very grave Injustice that is being dome to Canadians, especially to Canadians in the engraving business, bv the course pursued by the government. I have not made any charge that the work toeing done at present is not well done. I did not raise that question at all. 1 raised the question whether it was a good business proceeding, one that wmdd commend itself to the approval of any business man in Canada, that a contract involving $700,000 or $800,000 or $1,000,000 should have been entered into by this government, a renewal contract too, without their asking for competitive tenders. There is not a gentleman on that side of the House who. if his own money were at stake, would not seek by public competition to get the work done Iowa4 than it Is done now. But no Canadian firm has been given any opportunity to put in a tender. I do not profess to know as much as my horn friend from West Huron (Mr. Holmes) of the number of firms in Canada which are competent to do this work; but I repeat that if an opportunity had been given to Canadian firms to com-

pete for this work, more than two tenders would have been put in. I noticed that when this matter was up dm the House in 1897, a letter was read from Sir. George R. Barber, of Georgetown. He said that be and his associates would have put in a tender, If an opportunity had been given them. I do not know whether the hon. member for West Huron can give me any information about printing of this character. On certain classes of printing I will not take any information from him, though be may speak upon other classes. But I know that there are firms in Toronto and Montreal which, if opportunities had been given them, would have been only too glad to have put in bids for this work, and would have done just as good work and given just as good satisfaction as this American firm is doing; and I know no good reason why Canadian firms should not have been given that opportunity. If a proposition of this character had been submitted to bon. gentlemen opposite for their approval when they were on this side of the House, they would have been loud in their denunciation of it. It is not a business proposition nor one that ought to be supported by the members of this House.
I cannot state the! amount of the annual expenditure under each.
Could the minister get the information and give it to us at some later stage ?

Certainly.
Additional amount required for clerical assistance in connection with the issue and redemption of Dominion notes, $1,150.

In the course of a discussion which,took place in this House some time ago, a number of the members recommended the redemption of many of the notes which are in circulation. There is an opinion prevalent throughout the country that many of these old notes are not only very unclean, but tend to disseminate disease; and I am inclined to believe that there is some truth in that opinion. In fact, it is believed that small-pox has been transmitted by means of Dominion notes or bank notes sent through the mails. If that is the case, it seems to me a matter of importance that these old notes should be redeemed and replaced by new ones. Has the minister made any arrangement for that purpose, and if so to what extent ?

The difficulty lies, not with the government, but

with the public, who have the remedy in their own hands. The government issue notes with a view to providing the public with clean notes, and if the public will ask the banks for clean notes, -they will be entitled to get them. The government is not a bank of issue, but all the banks are supplied with clean bills.
Is there anything in the Bank Act that requires the banks to supply the public with clean notes ?
No, there is not.
Then it would be optional with the banks whether they would do it or not ?
They will always do it, if asked.

It seems to me that from a sanitary standpoint the time has come when the government should consider this matter seriously. I have consulted one or two medical gentlemen on the subject, and they are of opinion that the SI and $2 Dominion notes are most effective disseminators of disease. The $5 and $10 bills of the chartered banks are not quite so objectionable from a sanitary standpoint as the bills issued by the government, and it seems to me that the government should take some steps to see that the old bills are called in and cleaner bills issued in their place. The danger is one that does not exist to the same extent in European countries, where silver and gold are used more extensively as it does in this country and in the United States, where bills are the -common currency.

The hon. gentleman must surely understand that $1 and $2 bills are in very much more general circulation than $5 bills. Bills of $1 and $2 are very much more in circulation than those of $5. They are used continually and pass practically as change, whereas $5 bills are not used so often, and consequently are not so much defaced. As has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite, something should be done to enforce the calling in of those defaced and dilapidated bills. We have too many of them in this country. Besides it depreciates our bills in the United States. It is difficult enough to get our Canadian bills taken at par in the United States, and much more difficult when they are defaced and dilapidated. I do not know what remedy we could apply. As stated by the hon. the Postmaster General, the remedy is in the hands of the banks and the people who use the bills. If the people would return those worn-out bills and ask for gold instead, to which they are entitled, that possibly might bring about a change. It is a matter, in any case, which should receive the consideration of the government, and I hope the government will bring about a change, so that we will not have so many defaced bills in circulation as at present.

Last

House of Commons-additional amount required for stationery, $2,500.
I suppose this is in connection with our annual supply?

Yes,
under the control of the committee.

We had some supplies last year, in which there were a lot of nick-nacks which were of no use. Of course, some of the stationery was valuable, but some of the things supplied were merely an expenditure of public money to very little purpose.

Additional amount for publishing the debates,
That seems a very large amount to require at the end of the year.
That item could be considerably reduced if hon. gentlemen opposite would not talk so much.

I am not in a position to give the explanation, and the chairman of the Debates Committee is not present If the hon. gentleman wishes we will let the item stand.

Legislation-library-To provide statutory increases for two messengers, Albert Beaudry and Thomas Lynton at $30 each, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $60.

The POSTMASTER' GENERAL. I cannot give the hon. gentleman that information. The Library Committee, which is a joint committee, has made this recommendation.
Legislation - general- printing - Additional amount required, $35,000.
Is this to pay for contracts outside, or is it to meet expenses of the Printing Bureau 1
As this is for legislative printing, I take it that it would be for the Bureau.

Is there any minister present who can tell us whether we get much printing done outside of the Bureau ? We see the statement made In the press that that is the case. If we knew the facts, we should be better able to estimate whether the Bureau is as valuable as we anticipated that it would be.

For my own department, I have had only one item of printing done outside of the Bureau. That was a money order book, and it was done outside for the double reason of economy, and because the Printing Bureau had not the facilities and desired us to get it done elsewhere. I believe that some departmental reports, in cases of urgency, have been printed outside. The Secretary of State, who is in charge of the Printing Bureau, reports that the demand has outrun the facilities of the Printing Bureau and the premises should be enlarged. The King's Printer himself is compelled to request that some of the printing be done outside.
I see it stated in the press-it may not be correct, but I think it must be nearly correct or no editor would

publish it-that $75,000 was paid for printing to one newspaper company alone. It seems hardly economical to get our printing done outside when we have a Printing Bureau equipped and running, and all it needs is enlargement.
It would take a lot of money to enlarge it.
Well, $75,000 is quite a sum of money to ordinary mortals.
But after you pay for the enlargement, the printing costs money even if it is done in the Bureau. I understand the printing now required exceeds the capacity of the Bureau.
Then, enlarge the Bureau.
That is not so easily done.
It is as easy to do that as to spend these enormous sums in getting printing done outside.
No doubt it will come to that.
Then, it would be better if if came to it when the government have the money to spend. We all know that the pendulum will swing the other way and by and by, they will have less money.
But this is a government of economy, you know, and we do not wish to spend so much.

But, if the minister would explain more, and talk less it would save time. And I hope the hon. gentleman will accept that in as good a spirit as it is given. My contention is that it would be far better to spend the mon4y in enlarging the Printing Bureau now that the revenue is buoyant, rather than spend the money on printing outside and still have the Bureau incomplete when the revenues are lower. It would be better to spend the money in this way than in the-would it be unparliamentary, Mr. Chairman, to say in the foolish way, in which much of it is now spent ?
I guess we can stand that.

Here is the fact staring us in the face that the Printing Bureau needs enlargement. When the Postmaster General sat on this side of the House he used to tell us that the public buildings here were filled from garret to cellar with officials. And now, not only are these public buildings filled, but the government is spending $18,000 in rent for other buildings, and, unless they are renting buildings that they do not need, these also are filled from garret to cellar with officials. Would it not be better to provide proper accommodation in buildings owned by the government, instead of paying rent 7 And, in the same

way, would it not be better to enlarge the Printing Bureau than to pay these large sums for printing done outside ?

I thinls that, when we come to concurrence, information ought to be given as to what printing is done outside and what we pay for it annually, specifying the various lines of printing and giving the names of parties to whom the money is paid. The item we are now discussing is only one, and I suppose there are others in the main estimates for some other purposes. Also, we ought to know how many are employed in the Printing Bureau. Will the minister give this information on concurrence ?
As far as possible, yes.

For many years past the departmental reports have never been issued at as early a date as were the reports for the year ending 30th June last. This was due to the fact that the copy was sent to the Bureau in reasonable time. * Moreover, the copy was not sent in simultaneously so as to choke up the Printing Bureau, but was sent in in good time, and so the work was expeditiously turned out and the reports distributed much earlier than has been the practice for years. We have a very efficient and well equipped Bureau, but some additions will have to be made. Any one who knows anything about the Bureau will admit that the work can be done there as well and more cheaply than by giving it out to political friends of the government throughout the country. The Bureau was established for the very purpose of getting the work better done and more efficiently done, and the country is not getting the full advantage of the Bureau and of the large sums expended upon it if all the public printing is not done there. If it required a small additional expenditure to equip the Bureau even more efficiently than it is at the present time, the money would be well spent. An additional space is required for the work of the bindery, and an additional space for the press department. The expenditure of the small sum required to equip and complete these departments would enable a much larger amount of work to be done. It certainly can be done as efficiently and more economically than when it is given out. The Bureau ought to be employed to its full capacity in doing the public work.

speechtext:
In connection with the printing and distribution of the blue books,
I have been informed that there is a general complaint amongst the memtjers of the Conservative press in respect to the giving
out of these blue-books. Under the late government when a book was issued it was handed immediately to the members representing both political parties, at the same time. Now, the members of the Reform press are furnished with an advance copy a day or two before the Conservative press. That is the complaint made by the representatives in Ottawa of the Conservative press. The Reform reporters have the benefit of a day in advance. That is something that was never done under the late Conservative government.

Speaking under correction, I do not believe that this reported abuse can be substantiated. It may be there is an odd case, but that was not the intention at all events. The order is that all newspapers should be treated alike.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman will see that the order is carried out better.

I would like to know why it is that the ' Hansard ' printed in French is so late in being distributed to the members. I only see the French 'Hansard ' ten or twelve days after the speeches have been delivered, and during the recess I do not receive it for four or five months. I do not see why it should not be sent to us in a couple of weeks at least. Also in regard to the Auditor General's Report; I was down there a couple of weeks ago to see if there were any printed in French, and was told that they would not be ready for four or five months. If they are not ready for four or five months it is no use to have them at all. When we come here at the beginning of the session we cannot get a French report of any kind.

My hon. friend iknows that so far as the debates of the House are concerned, the government has nothing to do with them. That is a matter in regard to which he should lay his complaints before the Debates Committee, and I have no doubt the committee will look into it. With regard to the Auditor General's Report, I do not believe the fault lies with the Printing Bureau. If there is any delay in the work it must be occasioned by the translators, because I am pretty sure that as soon as the copy goes into the Bureau it is quickly disposed of.

I have been told by the translators that as soon as the House closes a good many of them are dismissed from the service. I was told so to-day. I was told that if they were kept on. a few weeks longer the French report would be printed in a couple of weeks.
Gratuities for ballot designs partially adopted,

The Secretary of State informs me that when the amended Franchise Act was passed we

adopted to some extent the designs of some gentlemen who had submitted ballots. Trade and Commerce-Bounties on iron and steel-to meet expenditure in connection with the administration of the Act, $2,000.
The administration of this Act, which was formerly in the Customs Department, is now transferred to Trade and Commerce.
This is to meet the cost of administration in connection with the bounties on iron and steel ?
