I do not know whether we can get the information in connection with this item, but I would like to know how much we are to pay this year for bounties on iron and steel. It was expected a year or two ago that the amount would run up very rapidly. That information will enable us to estimate the rate of progress that is being made in the output.

It has increased very rapidly. The amount for the current year will be very considerable, and the amount in the coming year will be very much larger. It will be far in excess of what we have yet paid. If my hon. friend desires the information I will have a statement prepared for concurrence.

I suppose the hon. Minister of Finance could scarcely give us much information as to the amount of trade that has been carried on as a result of our subsidizing this line, or as to whether we have been able to create a trade with France in addition to that which was hitherto carried on ?
I could not tell my hon. friend.

Up to the present time, I am sorry to say, I do not think it has resulted in developing very much business, but I may say that I hope we will be able to do better in the future. The expectations have not beeu realized that were entertained at one time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will that be enough ?
It is a very modest sum.

Will the right hon. Prime Minister be able to give us any information as to the line that will be followed at the conference ? Can he give the committee any information regarding it beyond what he has already given the House ?
My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) knows that upon the invitation of the Imperial government, the Prime Ministers of the self governing colonies will meet in London with the view of discussing

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
certain subjects. We have already given our views as to the character of the discussion which will take place at the conference. I should also say that at the initiation of the Canadian government a conference is to take place between the colonies of Australia. New Zealand and Canada. It has been decided that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) and the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) shall represent the government at that conference. As to what shall be the subjects which will be debated, I may say that the conference will be held with a view of developing trade between the self governing colonies, between Australia, New Zealand and Canada, and we hope we will be able to make arrangements with that end in view. As to that, however, we are in the dark yet. Australia has just adopted a new tariff and New Zealand has a tariff somewhat similar to our own. All their revenues are raised by customs duties. 1 believe from what I have been told by the hon. Postmaster General and from the report which has been placed on the Table of the House by the hon. Minister of Finance, that the prospects of our being able to do a large business in Australia looks very bright. Almost everything they require to supply themselves with, Canada can supply. New Zealand cannot perhaps afford such a large field but we hope also to do something there. We are of the opinion that if any trade can be developed we will probably have to subsidize a line of steamers, and we have thought, that possibly, by subsidizing a line of steamers between Canada and Australia, taking in South Africa, a large business might be developed. We have great hopes of South Africa. When the war is over, and the time cannot be very far off now, this country will require to be supplied with almost everything, and it is our intention to push matters in that direction as far as we can. My hon. friend asked me:	What
is the line I will take. 1 do not know that X can say much more than I have already said. The line must be general. We are there simply to offer and receive suggestions. The only thing we have in view is to develop trade by two means:	By trade
preferences and by subsidizing lines of steamers.
I suppose the Prime Minister will adhere to his determination that he will not discuss the defences of the empire.
I have not changed my mind upon that subject.
You do not want preferential trade, then ?
I would be-very glad to have it.

I do not know how far the Prime Minister may be able to
adhere to his present opinions, because if the premiers of the other colonies begin to discuss the question of defence, perhaps that question may be forced to some extent upon the premier of Canada. That is a subject in which we are all interested. I have been studying the tariff of the Commonwealth of Australia to some extent, and in the matter of dry goods I find that in several instances it is about 10 per cent less than our own tariff. The duties on carpets and flannels are 15 per cent, while our rates are nearly double that. I believe that this is an opportune time for Canada to extend her export trade to South Africa and to Australia. It is all very well for us to expound the sentiment of Canada for Canadians, but we will never build up a large export trade if we confine ourselves to that idea. For those who are complaining of the tariff in connection with the manufacture of woollen goods, 1 think this is the time for them to avail of the opportunity of extending their trade to these colonies. There must be direct communication to enable them to do so-I was going to say from the St. Lawrence-to South Africa and to Australia ; because it is impossible for them to send their goods to Vancouver en route to the east, and if they send their goods to New York they would have to pay the freight, and they would be met at once by the American manufacturers, who would have the advantage to that extent. The Americans are pushing their trade in Australia with great energy, and it is therefore to our advantage to encourage this trade now, so tliat Canada may get hold of a large portion of it. There is scarcely anything produced in Canada but there is a market for it in Australia, provided you have the means of conveying your goods direct from our own ports.

I was very much delighted to hear the remarks of the Prime Minister regarding his visit to England. When we speak of extending our trade to Australia ,and South Africa, it is of a great deal more importance for us at the present time to endeavour to do our own trade at home amongst our own people. How can we expect to export goods when we cannot even manufacture goods for our own people in Canada ? In one of our greatest industries we find our own market at the present time flooded with foreign goods and goods of British manufacture. The United States are doing a large business in Australia, but they first of all captured their own market and made their own market impregnable. Canada can never do a foreign trade while the Canadian market is being invaded in the very lines which we want to export. I read with a great deal of pleasure a letter from a gentleman in Australia-I think a son of the Hon. Mr. Ross-and that letter had many strong points in favour of our attempting to do business there, which ap-

pealed to me as a Canadian. But lie forgot, as our own government are forgetting, that we have not even got our own market. The government are so afraid of offending members on that side of the House who say they have come here with a mandate from the people to advocate free trade. Well, so long as they are afraid of that element, we can do no export trade from Canada. First of all, my advice, very humbly submitted to the Prime Minister, is to take every means to protect our own markets for our own people, and when we have risen to the elevation that the manufacturers of the United States have risen to, and when we commence to overflow with our own products, then we will be able to capture other markets. The time of the most talented business man who will go to England will be wasted in attempting to advocate a foreign business unless he can first say that we are supplying our own market. Until that is done, there is no use wasting time attempting to do a foreign business. You may subsidize all the steamers you like to Australia, but we must have a return cargo. You are preventing us from doing a woollen business in this country, and one of the great staples of Australia is wool. ITow can we use their wool if we cannot capture our own market for woollen goods. If you are going to give a preference, as our respected premier did to the manufacturers of Yorkshire-and Canada is just as much a part of the empire as Yorkshire is-you hamper us in our own market and you afford facilities to men who already have a great advantage in all the markets of the world. In order to enable us to do a foreign trade, we must have increased duties on certain lines of goods that we can manufacture here. When we have that, the Prime Minister can go in confidence to England, and he can talk to the other colonial delegates with something like business acumen. He can say to them : We are able to supply our own market; and they will not be able to throw in his face the remark: What are you talking about exporting goods to Australia for when you cannot supply your own market. I would humbly submit that this would be a better course for the premier than making all kinds of offers of preference. Let the right hon. gentleman provide, first of all, that the Canadian market shall be for the Canadian manufacturers.
The PKiiviE MINISTER. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) will not succeed in throwing cold water on my enthusiasm. I do not hope, and perhaps it would not be wise for me to hope, that we should take wool to Australia any more than we can carry coal to Newcastle.
I said manufactured wool.

There are other things besides wool. I do not see why we Mr. BROCK.
. should not take cotton to Australia, as well as to China, and I understand we have had an export cotton trade to China for some time, and that a profitable business was done in that line a few years ago.
What are Canadian cotton stocks to-day ?

We are at the present time sending agricultural implements to Australia, and we are pretty successful competitors with the Americans, and I think we can even do better. But, of course, if my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) says we must have a high tariff in this country. I despair of having any preferences. 1 always understood, however, the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite was that if they adopt protection in England, then we might hope to have a preference, but now I understand from the hon. gentleman that he wants a high protection against England as well as against the rest of the world, and no preference with the mother countrv. If the views of my hon. friend should prevail I cannot see any future for this country. 1 am sorry to say for my hon. friend, and happy to say for myself, that I hold altogether different views from him on this matter.

Excuse ime for a moment. We are holding out very great inducements to bring in immigrants into this country, and at the present time we are succeeding in getting thousands of settlers in the Northwest. Is the right hon. gentleman perfectly satisfied that we should be always hewers of wood and drawers of water ? Is he perfectly satisfied that we in the east should not supply manufactured goods to those people on whom we are spending thousands of dollars to induce to settle in the North-west ? If this country can double its population, we shall be in a far better position to make a trade arrangement with the other dependencies of the empire and with the empire itself than we can, situated as we are at the present time. I do not always take my politics from the United States, but in this matter of trade they have shown themselves wise in their day and generation. They have protected their market almost to prohibition, and they are the most successful nation on the face of the globe to-day. Weak-kneed politicians on the other side of the House disparaged a high tariff and kept on disparaging it. Fortunately they remained in opposition. Unfortunately for us, weak-kneed people are in control of the government to-day; but the right hon. leader of the government, surrounded as he is by business men, may depend upon it that sooner or later that kind of politics will come to grief in this country. The larger the influx of population, the greater is the necessity of our being able to supply them with our own goods. If we are going to maintain anything like a patriotic sentiment in this country, we

must encourage our .people to buy goods in the country. The hon. gentleman says we can export cotton to Australia. I happen to deal in cotton myself, and I know something about the cotton trade. It is simply ridiculous for us to suppose that we can compete with Great Britain in sending cotton to Australia. The United States invariably gains entrance to a foreign market by slaughtering goods at prices much less than they are sold at in the United States. That is the only way they capture a foreign market as against England. We must first protect and capture our own market. We might have a chance of selling woollen goods in Australia. That is one of the manufactures in this country in which we excel. Our woollen manufacturers have the best machinery in the world and the best workmen, and are to-day turning out as fine goods as are .made in any part of the world. But our market is so limited that we are not able to make the goods in sufficient quantities to make the business profitable. We only ask the government to give us our own market. If they would only experiment on that one line of woollen goods, I will guarantee that in three years they would find it so successful that they [DOT]would repeat the experiment in a great many other lines.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria,N.S.) , There is a Canadian woollen factory which is exporting woollen goods to Huddersfield, the very centre of the woollen manufacture in Great Britain. There are other things that can be exported to Australia besides woollen goods, which appear to be of so much interest to some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. There is one firm in Sydney, New South Wales, which would take a shipment of 2,000 tons of rolled paper for printing yearly. But that cannot be sent from here until we have direct communication. I saw it stated in * the papers that Canada is competing with Great Britain in Australia in agricultural implements, and I am sure that the Massey-Harris people are taking hold of the Australian trade very largely, and also the New Zealand trade. You will find their goods advertised in all the papers of those colonies. Then, a trade in boots and shoes, which are largely manufactured in Quebec and Montreal, could be cultivated there. You only require the steamers to carry goods backwards and forwards, and the trade will increase. When goods have to be sent via New York or via Vancouver over the Canadian Pacific Railway, it is impossible to extend our trade to that country.	[DOT]

The valuable advertisement we have had in South Africa will, I am sure, result in giving us a very important and valuable trade there, if we take time by the forelock, and push it as much as possible. There is no doubt that the quantity of goods sent from Canada to that country during the last year or two has given us an introduction which with a little care should enable us to hold and considerably extend that trade in the future. In Australia, a friend of mine is erecting saw mills which are manufactured in Brantford, Ontario; and in a letter received from him during the last few weeks he states that there is a magnificent opening there for a great trade in that line as well as in agricultural implements; and he suggests that direct steam communication between Canada and that country would enable that trade to be extended considerably. lie says that people came hundreds of miles to see the band saw and' the mill after it was set up, the first one in the country; and the immense timber areas there 'would afford an opportunity for a large trade in that line as time goes on.
For payment in connection with construction of Marconi wireless telegraph station at Glace Bay, N.S., in accordance with agreement, $70,000.
I thought we voted an amount for that already.
The contract price is $80,000, which has been divided into two parts-$70,000 in these estimates and $10,000 in the estimates for the coming year.
What in substance is the contract made with Marconi for establishing this station ?

The papers were brought down, but I can state it briefly to my hon. friend. At the time Mr. Marconi was in Newfoundland, and in consequence of the difficulty he met with there, through the objections of the cable company, when it appeared that his experiments in America were likely to be frustrated, we thought it a wise policy to invite him to come to Canada and continue his experiments with the view of establishing a station. He came, and was very much pleased with the courtesy extended to him by the government, and that led to our making the suggestion that Canada should participate in his undertaking; and it was agreed that we should contribute this much towards constructing the station, and that he should give us an engagement that if the experiment proved successful, as we hope and believe it will, his company would carry trans-Atlantic telegraphic messages for us very much below the current cable rates. For instance, where cable rates are 25 cents a word, he gave us an engagement that he would charge us not more than 10 cents a word.
While there is a possibility that it may not prove a commercial success, we consider ourselves justified in encouraging a man of great scientific attainments in carrying out an experiment which, if successful, will be of great advantage to the whole
This is a large sum.

This represents very large transactions. It will be remembered that at the beginning of our operations in the Yukon, when there were no banking facilities in that country, we arranged with the Bank of Commerce to act as our agent, and agreed to pay it si commission, to be fixed from time to time by the Minister of Finance. The bank had to be content to accept his judgment as to what was a fair commission. The first year we had to pay a high rate, I think as much as one and a half .per cent, but we have been reducing the rate from year to year. This vote represents, in the first part, a commission of three-quarters of one per cent, and in the second a commission of five-eights of one per cent, so that we have been gradually reducing the amount, as the conditions in the Yukon were brought nearer the ordinary conditions of banking in the older portions of Canada.
To pay Nelson R. Butcher, stenographer, for transcribing of evidence in Kloclc vs. Baring, $64.50.

That was incurred at the time of the Nipissing election. A mandamus was issued to the returning officer and a law suit resulted, in consequence of which we have to pay that amount to the stenographer. The Minister of Justice could give the particulars to my hon. friend if he were here.
That was when the returning officer took the liberty of postponing the election after he had put up the notices.

No, it was when he had a new writ sent to him and he had to do what he did.
To pay Messrs. Browning and Senkler, Klock vs. Baring, Nipissing election, $60,00.

As the Minister of Justice is not here, I would ask that the item be allowed to stand.

To pay expenses of Chinese and Japanese commission, $27,600.
Is there not another item in connection with that commission.
No, that will cover the whole expenditure.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Judging from the size of the report, it is very cheap.
What is the total cost of the commission ?
To pay one half arbitrators and stenographers fee Eastern Extension Arbitration, N.S., $3,952.62.

There was an arbitration consented to between the Dominion and the provincial government with regard to the claim which the province advanced to a share of the award, on the ground that it was made in the favour of the provinces. No provision was made in the estimates for paying the cost of the arbitration, and in the meantime the provincial government paid the arbitrators and claimed one-half of the expense. It was agreed that each party should pay his own share of the expenses. This deals entirely with the expense of the arbitrators and the stenographers, and as regards the other items, each party paid his own fees.

I suppose that this is ,one of these cases which we are likely to have for years to come. We are likely to have another claim of the same kind from Prince Edward Island next year. Is there any truth in the statement that they are preparing to make a large claim and expect to be compensated ?

My_right hon. colleague, the First Minister, made a statement the other day concerning this matter. There has been a somewhat hazy claim regarding the fishery award in the air a long time, but no understanding whatever has been arrived at between this government and the provincial government of Prince Edward Island. An intimation has been given that if. in consequence of the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as to the relative rights of the provinces and the Dominion, it is the

provinces and not the Dominion which should have received the award, then the fishery bounties which we have been allowing the provinces, and by means of which we have been practically paying them the interest on the award, will have to be stopped. Therefore, so far as the finances of the Dominion are concerned, the result that may be come to will be as broad as it is long. But no understanding whatever has been come to between the Dominion and the local governments upon the subject.

This was supposed to be a hazy account, but still, after a time it has materialized and we have to pay the money. Is the hon. gentleman aware of any claim having been made by the province of Quebec ? I saw an announcement to that effect in the local House.

There has been no time within the last ten or twelve years when some one or other of the provinces has not claimed that it was the provinces and not the Dominion which should have received the amount of the fishery award, and the claim is just in the same position as it has been at any time in the past. There will always be somebody in some provincial legislature who will raise the claim that the provinces should receive the money and not the Dominion, and of course we cannot prevent any such pretention being raised. But all I can tell the hon. gentleman is that there has not been any understanding whatever arrived at between the government and the government of Prince Edward Island or any other province on the subject. These provinces are free to follow whatever course they think best in these matters.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: There is usually a supplementary vote for the publishing of the debates. Last year, we asked $40,000. Generally the amount expended is $60,000. At the end of the session, we come to the House for a supplementary vote.

If the amount required is $60,000, would it not be better to put that amount in the main estimates, and then we would know. This looks as if it were a shortage, a case of emergency, and not a thing expected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I think that is a good suggestion. It ought to be done.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think that will do now.
Adjourn.

Charges of management-expenses in connection with the issue and redemption of Dominion notes, $70,000.
We were to get some information about this item so, perhaps, it had better be left over.
The Minister of Finance can give the information now.

It has been stated repeatedly that we have been paying very much less for this service than under the old contract. As the present contract has been renewed, the question arises how much we are paying now and how much we paid under the old contract; also for what length of time does this contract run.

We are paying in the aggregate more than we paid before, because the volume of business is greater; but we are paying lower rates than we were paying before. The contract has been laid on the Table, and all the details are available. The contract has been renewed for five years.
What is the aggregate of the contract ?

It is not for a lump sum, but for such quantities as we may need from year to year, and these are to be supplied at rates specified. As I say, they aggregate much more because we are using a very much larger quantity, but the rates are decidedly lower.

Printing, printing paper and binding, $110,uOO.
This is in connection with the Printing Bureau, and we were to get information on concurrence.
If the hon. gentleman will let it stand until it appears in the ' Hansard ' in the morning, so that we may see what is required.
We want to find out how much printing was being done outside, what we are paying for it, what departments it is done for, and the number of hands that are employed in the Bureau.
The order of my hon. friend is a large one, but I will do my best if the information is available.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think we had better stop here as I know the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has something to bring up.

I am sorry to find that the estimates have not yet arrived, and if we were to sit a little late I am advised that we could not get them. Under these circumstances I think we had better adjourn.
The PRIME MINISTER moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is to be the business to-morrow ?
We will take up all the Bills that remain on the Order paper, then we will go into the estimates for agriculture, immigration and the interior.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was the Prime Minister to give some information in reference to the Bill of the hon. member for Montreal, Ste. Antoine (Mr. Roddick) to-night ?
I told him I thought we could take it up to-morrow evening.
